speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, April 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the Government.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to engage in this debate on the budget. Since I realize that there is a certain amount of latitude allowed in the debate, I want to go on record now as stating how disappointed the Progressive Conservative Party is in the attitude of the New Democratic Party toward property rights when, on Friday, they refused unanimous consent to send the question of property rights to committee.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member must address the budget in the debate and not deal with completely extraneous matters.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) has barely begun his speech. The Chair is astutely conscious of the problem of relevance, as is any occupant of the chair.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am distressed that the NDP, having refused consent, now feel so concerned about the decision they made on Friday when they refused to allow the motion to be treated as a non-confidence matter, refused to allow it to go to committee and, in effect, refused to allow Canadians the protection of property rights in the Constitution.
I examined the budget from the perspective of my constituents. Simcoe North is representative of Ontario, being half urban and half rural, close enough to Metro Toronto to understand its problems but far enough away so that we do not get confused. For a nation with the promise that Canada has, we in Simcoe North are concerned about the way the country is suffering under the Liberals. Our economy should be leading the world. Canada's human and economic resources are second to none, but for too long Liberal administrations have pursued a "buy the vote now, our children pay later" policy. While the Liberals chased a Charter of Rights, Canadians watched their
jobs, their businesses, their homes, their farms, their hopes and their dreams slide down the drain.
Before discussing the budget directly, I want to address the general economic situation facing Canada on budget day. Our unemployment stood at 12.6 per cent, a post-depression record. We had youth unemployment at 21.3 per cent. Over two million Canadians were unemployed or had given up looking for work.
In Midland, Ontario, the Midland Free Press reported that a staggering 4,300 people were registered with the Canada Employment Centre. Midland has 33 per cent unemployment.
Canadians wanted a budget that would produce jobs, but they did not get it. Business bankruptcies in Canada in 1982 were 33 per cent higher than in 1981, 63 per cent higher than in 1980 and 91 per cent higher than in 1979. As we can see, business bankruptcies have doubled. The economy of the riding of Simcoe North is based on small business. Canadians wanted a budget that would address the problems of small business. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that they did not get it.
Home owners in Simcoe North, as did home owners everywhere, suffered through the horrendous mortgage interest rates created by the Liberal Party's high interest rate policy. Mortgage interest rates rose as high as 21 per cent and 22 per cent, causing misery to my constituents and to all Canadians during 1981 and 1982. Power of sale and foreclosure proceedings became the order of the day as a result of Liberal policies. Canadians were looking for a provision for the deduction of mortgage interest from taxable income or mortgage interest rate protection in the budget. They got neither.
As I have mentioned, Simcoe North is half rural and half urban. My farm constituents engage in beef and dairy cattle operations as well as in hog and lamb operations. My constituents also grow cash crops. During the past two years farmers have faced the problems that small business faced, including high interest rates and restricted credit. They were looking for a budget that addressed the problems of farmers. The budget did not do that.
What about the taxpayer? Disposable income has shrunk considerably due to inflation and high unemployment. The taxpayers in my riding were not looking for a budget that increased taxes, but it did. The budget increased taxes on the lower and middle class, not directly but in the traditional Liberal way, that is by deception.

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
People in Simcoe North were also concerned about the deficit. We do not want to mortgage our children's future with horrendous deficits; we want spending controlled. We want to eliminate the waste.
Given those problems facing us today, Mr. Speaker, what is our position on the budget? How do we view it? Did it address job creation, the problems of small business, mortgage interest rates, the plight of farmers, the lower and middle class taxpayer and the deficit? Those are the points on which I want to base my remarks today.
Faced with record high unemployment as a result of Liberal policies, what did the Finance Minister do to reverse the trend? First-and I approach this with some spirit that the Government has recognized something-the	Minister
acknowledged what Progressive Conservatives have been saying for years, namely that the private sector creates jobs, not the bureaucrats. I must admit that there is great interest in how the Finance Minister ever made the bureaucrats swallow that pill, but having swallowed it, let us look at the budget itself to see whether or not the Minister, in true Liberal tradition, was saying one thing and doing another.
The budget unveiled Special Recovery Programs designed to dazzle the Canadian people into thinking that the Liberals are doing something. The Liberals are going to spend $4.8 billion on capital projects next year. Of course, all Canadians realize that figure was originally $4.6 billion, which was adjusted overnight as a result of what is known colloquially throughout Canada as the "Lalonde leak". That is a good indication to Canadians of how much care went into the preparation of the program. We are asked to believe that this will accelerate the recovery of the economy. In fact, we all know that it is another Liberal pork-barrel scheme to buy votes and favours.
[DOT] (MIS)
The area of Midland-Penetanguishene will be shocked to find that the ILAP designation has been eliminated in the budget. After three months of waiting for that designation, after all the time and money spent on its application, the hopes and dreams of those people were dashed by the Government when it abandoned the ILAP concept.
We honestly thought that the Liberal Government would understand the crying need to create jobs in Canada. Once again we are amazed that they do not. Instead of quick and easy programs designed to encourage business, to hire people and to train them with a minimum amount of fuss and paperwork, we are besieged with short-term projects of devious long-range value. The programs referred to under the budget initiatives boggle the mind. Their end value as vehicles for employment are doubtful.
However, I would suggest that the enrolment of 5,000 young people in the reserve and regular forces of the Canadian Forces is a step in the right direction. In my opinion those young people will be enrolled and learning a trade and preparing themselves to make a contribution to Canada long before the bureaucrats in Ottawa have designed the forms for the other so-called job-creation programs. After all that, after enunciating the fancy programs, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) admits that unemployment will average an unacceptable 12.4 per cent in 1983 and that there will be 55,000 fewer jobs in 1984 than there were in 1981. What a sad commentary on an economic statement which, in the words of the Minister of Finance, was to help more than 1.5 million Canadians who want to work but cannot find jobs.
What did the budget do for small business? Canadians know that the Liberal Party is responsible for the current joke about small business: "Do you want to own a small business while the Liberals are in power? That is easy, buy a big one and wait." As I suggested, the investment tax credit provisions are complex. They presume the availability of funds to make investment and thus qualify for the tax credit. In fact, the available capital of small business has been severely impacted as a result of the Liberal-created recession. Small business has very little money to invest.
The other investment provisions are, in my opinion, for stockmarket investors, not for small business. What about the Federal Business Development Bank? I see the Minister responsible for small business in the House today. I understand he will make an announcement when he speaks, so let me deal with that announcement. What about the noises concerning what will be done through the FBDB? As a lawyer who worked with small business until becoming involved in politics, I want to say that when I see the Federal Business Development Bank doing something for small business, that is when I will believe it; not with announcements, not with brochures, but when I see it actually doing something for small business.
Let me quote from a letter I received from a constituent that deals with the Federal Business Development Bank, the "people's bank":
As you have been advised, prior to the completion of our investigation of your request for financial assistance the Federal Business Development Bank will require a prepaid commitment in the amount of $3,950.
That is the kind of help we are giving small business. It is a bank of last resort. If you are going broke and have $3,950, it will look at what you are doing. If the Liberals are serious about helping small business, they will act immediately to improve that image. They will put money into loans, not bureaucrats who pretend they understand business.
When the Minister makes the announcement about the Federal Business Development Bank becoming an investment bank and taking shares in small business, the question I will have for the Minister is how will the FBDB maintain its objectivity as a banker when it puts on the investor's hat? Why, when it is not the policy of the chartered banks in Canada to ask for a commitment from small business before looking at a loan proposition, is the Federal Business Development Bank demanding that kind of money?
Lastly, under the guise of helping small business, I want to deal with the loss carryforward provisions, called the loss carryovers. The Minister makes a big deal about increasing the loss carryover provision as a boon to small business. The
May 2, 1983

suggestion is that this will provide increased certainty to firms so that they can benefit more effectively from tax losses that they sustain. That is ridiculous. What kind of economy operates on the hope of tax losses? What kind of businessman or woman is proud of tax losses and wants them so they can carry them forward? I suggest to the Liberal Party that if they tell that to any bank manager in any small branch, they will laugh. That is what the business community will do to the Liberal Party with that provision.
Let us now move on to homes. The Minister of Finance helped the well-to-do invest in the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan. They are encouraged to release funds for the purchase of homes, furniture and appliances. What about the great bulk of Canadian home owners, the home owners who suffered through the Liberal high interest rate policy years? They are ignored. There is no provision in the budget to protect home owners against the ravages of high mortgage interest rates. Our policy, well stated and well enunciated, is that Canadians should be able to write off mortgage interest against other income. We would also consider mortgage interest rate insurance. However, the budget completely ignores Canadians who pay 20 per cent and 21 per cent on homes as a result of the high interest rate policy.
1 suggest that Canadians who presently own homes will not forgive the inaction of the Liberal Party from 1980 to 1982. We cannot allow the wrath of power of sale and foreclosure proceedings to continue to visit Canadian home owners without mercy. It may be Liberal policy, but it certainly is not Conservative policy.
What about the farmers? After the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), the most embarrassed Minister of this Government on budget night had to be the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). The budget is an insult to farmers. The only thing they are promised is the great boondoggle-being able to carry their losses back further and forward further. Isn't that an incentive? One can see the bureaucrats on Sparks Street coming up with that line. The budget proposed changes to enhance the ability of all farmers and Fishermen to utilize losses in one year to reduce taxes in the other year. In other words, they intend to see that these people keep losing money which they can write off over a longer period of time. That is nonsense.
At the same time as the Minister of Finance is promoting farm losses to enhance farming as an occupation, he is ignoring a very real problem. I refer to Section 31 of the Income Tax Act which states that farmers who incur losses on their farming operations are denied the opportunity to apply that loss to reduce non-farm income in excess of $5,000. In other words, the loss is levelled out to $5,000, a 1960 figure. Many of my constituents in Simcoe North have two jobs. They work very hard at farming and of necessity work on a full or parttime basis at another job.
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that farmers do not farm to lose money. Because of the Government's interest rate policy and lack of concern for the farming community, farmers are losing more than $5,000 a year and yet are working off the farm as well. When will the Liberal Government wake up to the reality of the situation in this country? When will it understand what is going on out there? Mr. Speaker, we support the review of Section 31 of the Income Tax Act in order to bring it up to modern day standards.
What did the Minister of Finance do to the taxpayer on budget night? I am interested in what he did for the middle and lower income Canadians who foot the bill of the Government for Liberal wastefulness. He increased taxes. Federal sales tax will be increased by one percentage point October 1, 1984. Tax exemptions for children will no longer be indexed for inflation. The federal tax reduction will be reduced. The standard deduction of $100 for charitable donations will be removed. The Canadian ownership special charge will be maintained, although we have no plans to buy anything. Telecommunications charges will be subject to a 6 per cent sales tax.
Only a Liberal Finance Minister could increase the taxes of lower and middle income Canadians and then claim that the economy will improve because lower and middle income Canadians will spend more money as consumers. It is twisted logic, but then again, the definition of Liberal logic is twisted logic.
What about the deficit? What is $31.3 billion? That is the projected deficit. It is more than Ottawa spent in total in 19741975. A $31.3 billion deficit is equal to $3,120 per taxpayer, $1,200 for every man, woman and child in Canada. One tax dollar in three goes to service the debt. Given that problem, what did the Minister do to address it in the budget? Nothing. There is no indication of restraint in the budget. There is no provision in the budget to cut spending, just a provision for future spending. The Government is gambling. It is gambling that revenues will increase rather than taking action to control and reduce spending.
Government spending was up 17.6 per cent in 1981-1982; 16.8 per cent in 1982-1983, the year of the six and five provision; and it will go to 12.7 per cent in 1983-1984. When will the Government balance its books? Similary, the Government accepts the fact that over 12 per cent of Canadians will remain out of work. That is a national tragedy.
On budget night the budget looked reasonable to us but detailed examination of it has revealed the usual Liberal flimflam. It contains no depth of stimulation, no depth of concern. Once again, the Liberals have failed to help the unemployed, small business people, farmers, the home owner and the lower and middle class.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Are there any Hon. Members rising to ask questions of the Hon. Member who has just spoken? If not, the Chair recognizes the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Rompkey).

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Rompkey
Hod. William Rompkey (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)): Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by thanking my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), for the particular attention he has paid to my client group, the medium-sized businesses of Canada. As I have travelled across the country in the past months to speak with business people, it has become clear that there were a number of specific issues that could be dealt with in the budget that would go a long way toward helping this dynamic part of our economy play a major role in the economic recovery. I am pleased to say that the budget incorporates many of those measures.
My own Committee, the Consultative Committee on Small Business, has been discussing many of these initiatives over the past few months. They were of the view that the adoption of these initiatives would provide a significant stimulus to this segment of the private sector and contribute to our industrial and regional economic development objectives. I could not help but be pleased to see how many of the recommendations that I made on behalf of the Small Business Consultative Committee became part of the budget. There is a growing awareness of the tremendous value of small business to Canada's economic well-being. Perhaps these businesses do not stand out individually, with some particular exceptions, but collectively they provide the base on which our industrial strength stands. The analogy would be to compare it to a hockey game. The superstars get all the credit but they could not do their job unless the rest of the team did theirs.
I believe this budget will significantly help small business do its job. Clearly, a first priority was to take action directed at providing employment. Bringing forward a number of major capital projects will project a stimulus into the economy in the short term. These undertakings have their own direct, beneficial impact. They also have a spin-off impact on the small business community which supplies the needs of the larger firms. This group will benefit from the pick up in demand.
At the same time the budget recognizes another immediate need-the need to provide assistance to companies that have undergone a tremendous period of pressure during this global recession. Smaller firms were particularly hurt through this period. They do not have internally generated resources to draw upon to the same extent as large firms and they do not have the same access to externally generated funds. The Minister of Finance has been sensitive to this debt-equity problem of small business.
I must concur with the Minister of Finance when he said:
The way in which so many have managed to pull through the recession is a tribute to the dedication and entrepreneurial spirit of Canadians.
He was referring to small firms which he described as "one of the most dynamic and innovative elements in the private sector". The budget takes a number of positive measures that will enable our small firms to restore their balance sheets. It is the first step necessary to provision themselves to take advantage of the economic recovery now building momentum.
Improving the investment climate and increasing the availability of internally generated funds will allow our industries to invest in innovative activities. These are the very activities that Canada needs most to ensure our competitive position both at home and in world markets.
I should like to draw the attention of the House to the way the specific measures in the budget are of benefit to small and medium-sized firms. While the provisions are beneficial to all Canadian industries, I believe that small business people can see themselves singled out as a major vehicle of our economic recovery.
The measures addressing business losses will provide a major improvement to the cash flow of businesses, increasing the carryback to three years instead of one and providing the alternative of carrying losses forward for seven years instead of the previous five. This will have an immediate impact on small business. More important, this measure will stabilize the small business cash flow once the recovery takes hold and profitability returns. The provision for the carryback of capital losses to be increased to three years from one will have a similar impact and will improve a company's cash flow.
Additional changes, such as removing the upper limit of the investment tax credit, will be welcomed by small business. So too will be the provision for the remission of a portion of the tax credit directly to the business. This, of course, provides significant benefit to those firms without taxable income. It is a major measure in view of the serious erosion of small business profits in the past year.
As the House is aware, the budget proposes to refund 40 per cent of our new tax credits directly to the firm. This will be particularly valuable in assisting firms to finance research and development or purchase certain manufacturing, transportation and construction capital assets. Firms that combine this measure with the tax credit to purchase common shares will find that they are able to reduce their cost of new equity issue. The tax credit to common share purchasers will also encourage the injection of new permanent capital and liquidity into businesses. This must happen if companies are to redress their serious debt to equity ratio problems. It has been a longstanding problem for smaller businesses to raise equity. This budget measure, by appealing to venture capitalists and individuals, will help overcome that problem.
Hon. Members will also note that the Minister of Finance proposed a number of measures for discussion that will enhance the ability of firms, particularly small firms, to benefit from R and D tax incentives and to attract financing for R and D ventures.
In my discussions with the small business community in Canada it was clear that its major request was that its needs should be addressed through the tax system. The small business community was saying that the programs are there but people did not necessarily have the time to read the brochures and fill out the applications. It was asking for a break within the tax system. It held that this approach would provide the
May 2, 1983

framework within which it could adjust to its own particular circumstances. I am pleased to note that the budget does exactly that.
That is not all the budget has done to assist small business; other specific measures will also be beneficial. I note the increase in funding for the program of export market development and would point out to the House that the principal beneficiaries of this measure will be small businesses. The Government has repeatedly stressed the value of exports to our economy. It is perhaps not well known that small firms play a major role in our export business. To encourage even more participation-because it is particularly difficult for small businesses to break into this highly competitive area-additional funding is being made available.
Here in Canada, the construction industry will be particularly helped by the budget. The Minister of Finance has provided an additional $355 million to speed a continued recovery in the housing industry as well as the funds that will be spent as part of the Special Recovery Capital Projects Program. I point out to this House that almost 97 per cent of the construction firms in Canada are small businesses. It is evident that they will benefit significantly.
Also in the budget, I am pleased to note, is a proposal that responds to another major consideration of small businesses. The Minister of Finance, in responding to a request from many associations and groups, announced that the Canada Tax Foundation will hold a national symposium this summer on the subject of simplifying the tax system. As a former Minister of Revenue I applaud that. As we know, simplifying a tax system is far from a simple process, but I look forward to participating in this endeavour that will be of such benefit to Canadian firms.
In his budget address the Minister indicated that I would be providing information on the expanded role of the Federal Business Development Bank. The Bank has long played a valuable role in assisting the needs of smaller businesses. As it evolved from its beginning as the Industrial Development Bank, the need to modify the Bank's role became evident.
I am announcing today that the Federal Business Development Bank, while maintaining its traditional functions of term lending, will expand and refocus its client services and progressively embark on its role as a merchant banker. This latter role will enable the bank actively to identify new business ventures and participate in their development. In doing so, the FBDB will usually take a minority position with the intention of selling the shares after a few years. The Bank's new role will continue to focus on the needs of the small firms and it will complement the tax measures outlined in this budget. Taken together, the two thrusts will substantially improve the business environment for Canadian firms.
The basic service of the Bank has been term lending and this will continue. At the same time we must recognize that the Bank has been facing increasing competition from Canadian chartered banks and other lending institutions in this area. That is as it should be. In fact, I believe that the Federal Business Development Bank has, in a way, been instrumental in creating this competition for itself. By demonstrating that
The Budget-Mr. Rompkey
term lending can be profitable in a number of cases that the other institutions had already rejected, it caused these other institutions to re-examine their practices. Their examination obviously led them to conclude that many Canadian firms who had already been turned down were in fact good prospects.
As a consequence, as I have noted, commercial institutions have moved to increase their lendings to smaller firms on terms which they can afford. I would hope that the role of FBDB as a catalyst will continue, believing as I do that Canadian banks can go much further in their efforts to help the smaller firms.
I have met with the Bankers' Association and I am meeting with each bank individually. In those meetings I have asked them to review their collateral demands which, I believe, are often excessive and to consider additional training of their staff in how to deal with the special needs of smaller firms. I have stressed to them that there appear to be different levels of service across Canada, with firms in British Columbia and Newfoundland expressing particular concerns.
There is one consequence of the increase in term lending by the banks which we cannot ignore. FBDB has increasingly moved to provide term lending to higher risk firms. It is clearly the lender of last resort for Canadian companies and is, therefore, the institution which is running the greatest risk. It is reasonable, then, to expect that it will incur losses in its term lending portfolio. When one considers that the chartered banks, with their choice of loans and their emphasis on collateral, incurred losses in 1982 of $1 billion more than they had anticipated, it is evident that the FBDB would have even greater problems. I believe this is a reasonable cost of doing business with the Government operating in partnership with Canadian firms. If we had no losses, I would believe we were not taking sufficient risk.
The Bank does not restrict itself to term lending. Without question, a major need for many Canadian small businesses is information and advice about the management of their operations. Additional funding will be provided so that FBDB's current business and information services can be expanded. The client services offered by the Bank have proven invaluable to many firms in the establishment of their long-term viability. The Bank will particularly emphasize the delivery of these services outside the major urban centres of Canada. So we hope, Mr. Speaker, that the FBDB will particularly focus on small business and on small business in rural Canada. Small businesses will be assisted in the preparation of their proposals which they will be taking to the private sector financial institutions. In this way we will be meeting a demonstrated need and, I hope, will also spur the chartered banks to greater effort in this regard.
These services must be offered at a cost which smaller firms can afford, and to do this the Bank has traditionally subsidized this service from the profits made on its term lending role. As I have pointed out, these profits will be harder and harder to achieve as the other lending institutions move into areas that

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Rompkey
the FBDB has shown to be money makers. In spite of this, we believe this service to be invaluable to the Bank's clients and as a consequence the costs must be absorbed.
The progressive expansion of the "merchant banking" function of the FBDB will Fill this gap which exists for small firms seeking financing. As the Bank develops its investment banking capability FBDB will address the equity and other financial requirements of promising small businesses. These are the very businesses upon which we depend for innovation but for whom the raising of equity presents the greatest difficulty. Essentially, the Bank will be a deal maker for these smaller firms. It will package financing arrangements for a fee or it may participate directly as an equity partner or holder of stock options.
In conclusion, I repeat that I believe this budget recognizes the tremendous value of small businesses to our economy. These firms will play a significant role in leading us on our road to recovery. They have the flexibility to move quickly into promising new ventures. They are the innovators who provide new products and processes. They are the network of suppliers who enable larger firms to continue. It has often been noted that employment creation is largely done by Canada's smaller enterprises. This budget, by providing significant assistance to them, will clearly assist us to achieve our overriding goal, that of providing long-term, meaningful work to Canadians in all parts of the country.
Again, I congratulate the Minister of Finance for presenting the small businesses of Canada with a package of tax measures and other stimulative initiatives which will enable them to grow and flourish. This budget has responded to the needs of, and to the requests made by, the small business community. When they take advantage of the opportunities which are presented, as I am sure they will, Canada's industrial capability will be enhanced.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Minister responsible for small business. In a letter from the Federal Business Development Bank to a constituent of mine it was stated, in part: "Prior to the completion of our investigation of your request for financial assistance, the Federal Business Development Bank will require a prepaid commitment in the amount of $3,950". By contrast, the standard practice of the Canadian banking system, as received this morning from the Director of Public Affairs, is: "It is not standard practice for the chartered banks to level a commitment or standby fee on loans". The only exception might be in the case of a large multi-million dollar loan with a fixed rate.
Will the Federal Business Development Bank abandon its practice of requiring commitment fees from Canadians who go to them for loans?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before commenting on the particular instance, I would like to receive the details from the Hon. Member. I can assure him that I will take it up with the Bank. I would say in general that the people to whom I am listening, who are on the Consultative Committee which I have
and, moreover, the study done by the Federation of Independent Business, which is certainly not the great defender of the chartered banks has shown that collateral was too high and that service was not given to small business, particularly in the rural areas where there was no competition. My effort has not been to get FBDB to respond to small business because, indeed, they have been responded to by and large. For example, 23 per cent of the portfolio of FBDB is in tourism, which is essentially all small business.
I will be glad to look into the individual case which the Hon. Member has raised because I know of his sincere concern in this area. I do feel, however, that the reality is that in the past FBDB has been a lender of last resort but has been focusing on small business; and in my speech this morning I pointed out that we want them to do even more of that in the future.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is: Will the Federal Business Development Bank abandon its practice of charging commitment fees?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not aware that it is the practice of the Bank to do this. I undertook to look into this particular case, but I do not want to comment further on it until I have had a chance to examine exactly the point the Hon. Member is raising. As far as I know, however, it is not the practice to do that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we all listened with interest to the announcement of the Minister of State for Small Businesses concerning the terms of reference being changed for the FBDB and the re-focusing, to use his words, I believe, of banking interest into the business community; that is to say, taking minority positions or inventing for equity in the small business. It is shades of Nordair or Maislin Trucking, where you go into a situation in dire straits, invest money and in return take an interest. It is shades of General Motors, and on and on the list goes.
My question to the Minister is a very direct one. Is there an opportunity in those investments in small business by the Federal Business Development Bank for the business to purchase back without bonus, without penalty and without notice? In other words, if they invest in the company in order to bail it out of its difficulty, as a Government moves into the private sector, can the private sector buy back without notice, bonus or penalty?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is important to recognize the main thrust of this budget. The main message here is that if recovery is to come, and it will, then private enterprise has to be the main engine of the economy. To go even further, I would say that small business is the drive shaft, and that is exactly what we are emphasizing here this morning.
The main point is, however, that the preferred option, obviously, is to let the private sector do the job. If it needs some help, then how is that help going to be given? In the whole process of merchant banking, I do not think the first option would be to take an equity position. Possibly if there is other capital available from private sources, that might be the preferred option, and in my opinion would be. I have seen
May 2, 1983

certain cases in my own area, although I do not know whether the Hon. Member has seen them in his area, where unless that is done, the deal just does not fly. So there is a provision here for taking an equity position.
I do not think we should necessarily target that as being the first option, because I repeat that the main thrust is to let private enterprise do the job wherever possible. As far as unloading afterwards is concerned, I mentioned in my speech that there were certainly provisions for doing that and I would hope it would be done as easily and as quickly as possible.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that question was not answered satisfactorily. The question was a very direct one. If the Government is to take an equity interest in the private sector for the purposes of bailing out that business or helping it over a difficult period in its economic development, is the Minister prepared, as the Minister responsible for small business, to assure the House and the Canadian business community that there are no strings attached in a permanent investment by the Government of Canada into the private sector? In other words, will the Minister guarantee the House that that equity can be purchased back by the business from the Government without notice, bonus or penalty? What could be more simple than that question? Answer yes or no.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The answer is that it can be purchased back from the Government. With regard to the details of how that will be done, I would say to the Hon. Member that in the next couple of days I hope to give more details of the change in the FBDB. However, the general answer to the question is "yes", without saying "yes" to each one of the individual points which he raised, because within the next couple of days I hope to make a more specific announcement as to exactly how these functions will be carried out.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the problems which now seems to be confronting many smaller, older municipalities is that plants which have been the mainstay of employment in those municipalities are now closing and moving away, sometimes moving to other municipalities, sometimes closing entirely and just moving out of the country. I can see nothing proposed by the Government in its budget which begins to address that question. The question really involves responsibility to the municipality for the money which was spent in developing the infrastructure from which the company benefited, responsibility to the workers and their families who are totally disrupted and, in many cases, destroyed by the decision, without being given adequate notice or opportunity to participate in any discussion or decision making.
Does the Minister not feel that we have reached a point in time in this country when corporate behaviour must be altered somewhat and we must place some additional demands on those who make very important economic decisions which affect not only individuals but also entire communities? If so, would he subscribe to the idea that there might be some need to demand from the corporate dicision makers, large and
The Budget-Mr. Donald W. Munro
small, that they sit down, well in advance of a decision to close, so as to discuss the problem with their employees, municipal officials and various levels of Government, and to discuss the way in which they are reaching their decision so that the solution might be found and those companies are not placed in the position of having to move and the employees are not placed in the position of probably being unemployed, perhaps some of them for the rest of their lives?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is first of all important to point out that the budget will hopefully help companies to expand. Whereas companies have suffered losses before and have had to close down, the budget may indeed make others change their minds. People in my constituency are saying: "Look, have the companies looked at these new tax provisions? Maybe they can change their minds. Maybe they can take advantage of these provisions and rethink the whole process." Some closedowns may be affected because of the tax provisions here, but I do agree that the private sector has responsibilities, not only in getting the economy moving, but also in letting people know of their exact plans. There is a responsibility to the community. I know of cases where banks have pulled out local branches. It is the only game in town. One cannot pull out the hospital or the school.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That's right.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
However, one can pull out the banks. I think banks have some responsibility to provide a service. They should not simply take money out of the community but should show some responsibility toward it. The same kind of responsibility applies to corporations. I might even say that it applies to Crown corporations. They have not always been the most responsive to the needs of communities either, even though they are creatures of the Government.
I think the point is well taken, but I do not think we should be focusing on the past. Hopefully, things that have happened in the past might be rethought in the light of the budget provisions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The period of questions and answers has expired.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, basically I have two main threads to follow in my remarks today, the first being specifically directed to some of the unusual features surrounding and, indeed, leading up to the presentation of the budget of April 19. The second, while more general, is still related to the conduct of the Government in the fiscal field and its effects on economic recovery.
The springboard, if I may use the term, for my first series of comments was that utterly childish but, at the same time, rather frightening melange of arrogance, pettiness and teenage tomfoolery indulged in by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on Monday, or perhaps it was Tuesday, a fortnight ago, once he had bought his new shoes. I refer, of course, to his date with the cameraman. This was followed, as we all remember, by a quite unbelievable sequence of arrant stupidities

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Donald W. Munro
which could have been either intentional or the result of poor staff work. Again, I refer to the tabling first of one set of budget papers, followed by another, and finally, it would seem, by a third and possibly even a fourth.
The sleight-of-hand involved or the bad staff work calculated to cover up an inexcusable slip brought on by the arrogance to which I have already referred, or which was perhaps intended to do not more than lay this sort of smokescreen or create a diversionary issue around the matter, ended up in an exhibition of such sniggering self-justification on the part of the Minister as to be an egregious insult, I suggest, to the proprieties and the dignity of the House. It will stand forever as a blot on the record the Minister of Finance.
This was indeed a budget of recovery, as it was called by the Minister. It was fixed up at the last minute in an effort to effect the recovery of the Minister from an unpardonable lapse from orthodox parliamentary practice. At the last minute he quite obviously fudged the books by adding an extra $200 million to his proposed expenditures. He did not have time, however, to determine either where the $200 million was to be spent-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Job creation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-or from whose pocket it was to come. In this fashion he tried to extricate himself unscrupulously from a very sticky and thoroughly demeaning situation, that of exposing his budget in public before budget night. Surely a case of indecent exposure. I will leave it at that for a moment.
Yet this performance, planned or not, contrived or simply stumbled upon or into, was, in a manner of speaking, no more than the most recent in a sequence of events surrounding budget presentations. I hesitate to suggest that it could be the culmination but it was at least the last in a three-year series of distortive manipulations of the rules and traditions of the House surrounding budgets, their presentation and their consequences.
With all due respect, before the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Rompkey) leaves the Chamber, I would suggest that he contrived another one today. He might more properly have introduced his suggestions on Statements by Ministers in order to allow a debate. Instead, like some other Ministers, he worked it into his budget speech and had only ten minutes of questions. As I say, this is probably not the culmination but just one in a series.
Not content with playing with the documents that had to be tabled, the Minister of Finance announced one or two days later that the whole business of budget secrecy was outmoded and we should follow the U.S. practice. As far as the U.S. practice is concerned, I hope his staff will bring to his attention the comments made in a letter published in The Globe and Mail on April 27 by the Hon. Eugene Forsey in which he indicated that there is no possibility of drawing a parallel between that performance and the United States practice.
Of course, the Minister reversed himself on the logic of that comment by suggesting in a later comment that the T.V. cameraman whom he had teased and tormented even to the length of suggesting that he might like to use his zoom lens, was no better than a thief. Who is to say what other monstrous charges are still to come after that suggestion?
The history of budget presentations by this Government is not a very reputable one on other accounts, because it is breaking new ground in parliamentary tradition, whether intentionally or not, by allowing a single session to extend beyond three years. That is a revolution in itself. It is a record for which the Government, or at least some of its Ministers, are apparently unaccountably proud. Today is the five hundred and first sitting in our fourth year of this first session of the Thirty-second Parliament. However, that is another story which will have to be saved for another day because the mess surrounding the budget presentation is what we are concerned with here. Whether a parliamentary session extending into a fourth year is legal is a completely different issue.
To return to the budget, matters arose as far back as April, 1980 when the then Minister of Finance who is presently the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), used most of his time during the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne on April 21, 1980 to introduce a mini-budget statement-it is even called that in the Hansard index-and a Ways and Means motion. This is to be found at page 243 of Hansard of April 21, 1980. This is probably the first time that a Ways and Means motion has been introduced in such a manner.
This is only the first break with parliamentary traditions in the fiscal field during this session. The record over the next three years is just as startling, as I propose to outline.
A question of privilege that followed from that unusual performance in April of 1980 was raised by Members from this side of the House, because to accept such a practice without comment was to deprive Members of their rights to consider the budgetary proposals that were then being outlined. That is an important point. The debate on the address was almost completely concluded by that time and the Minister, therefore, was not subjected to questioning on the presentation of his mini-budget. Paragraphs 516 and 517 of Beauchesne were extensively quoted but to no avail, as seen by the ruling of the Speaker at page 459 of Hansard of April 28, 1980.
The next unusual performance with respect to budget presentations which I believe deserves being recounted occurred on October 28, 1980 when, in addition to announcing proposals to increase sales and excise taxes, customs tariff changes and changes in unemployment insurance premiums both for employees and employers, the same Minister of Finance then sneaked in an entirely new program under the guise of taxation proposals, one which has come to be known as the National Energy Program, a plan to governmentalize the energy industry.
It is a program that has had at least two serious consequences, as we are now finding out. First, it drove a great deal
May 2, 1983

of exploration activity out of the country and thereby deferred sine die the achievement of one of the laudible objectives of the plan, namely energy self-sufficiency. Second, it aggravated in a needless way and to an unusual degree our relation with offshore investors except, I must add, those who would be overwhelmingly advantaged before very long by the govern-mentalization process. An example of this is the acquisition of the Canadian operation of a foreign owned chain of service stations at inflated prices. Of course, I refer to Petro-Canada's acquisition of Petrofina at a cost of $1.6 billion which was in itself a gross overpayment for a static service station asset. This governmentalization proposal made in the course of that budget presentation was a further departure from the normal practices of the House.
We next come to the budget of November 12, 1981, still in the same session of Parliament, 20 months into the Thirty-second Parliament. We must remember that this was the budget that was torn to shreds bit by bit, as the days went by, by the very Minister who presented it. In all, some 90 changes were announced to the budgetary proposals that had been made public on the night of November 12.
mis budget of November 12, 1981 was eventually approved, if that is the right word, on December 8. It was approved but nibbled away at as though by mice. There were 90 changes to a budget that was approved. What, then, is the value of approval? What are Government backbenchers doing supporting their Government and then watching it shoot that approval full of 90 holes? Is there no honour left in this House? I am compelled to ask that question.
Even the budgetary deficit forecast in that budget of November, 1981 was repudiated in the Minister's next budget of June 28, 1982, which was some 26 months into the same session. In the previous November the Minister had forecast a $10.5 billion deficit. By June, only eight months later, he was obliged to announce that that deficit had almost doubled, from $10.5 billion to $19.6 billion, and that the financial requirements, instead of being the $6.6 billion announced in November, 1981, had virtually tripled to $17.1 billion only eight months later.
The budgetary process was obviously breaking down in a number of ways. Its provisions were being altered and withdrawn. Its forecasts both as to deficits and expenditures were being completely revised.
Another mini-budget was introduced by the new and present Minister of Finance on October 27, 1982. This was done by means of a statement introducing a Bill to secure authority to borrow an additional $4 billion. Again it was a break in tradition and an outright denial by the Government of the right of Parliament to discuss budgetary proposals when they are made. Bill C-128, the borrowing authority Bill, was passed within the week. It was approved by the silent majority on the other side of the House on November 2, 1982.
On December 7, 1982, a month later, Bill C-139 was introduced to amend the income tax law as a result of the provisions of the June budget. That Bill was not passed until
The Budget-Mr. Donald W. Munro
March 24, 1983. It received Royal Assent on March 30, 1983, the day the Easter break began.
What do you think happened next, Mr. Speaker? The next chapter of the budget saga began. Believe it or not, five days after the income tax Bill had been given Royal Assent, the Minister made public a document entitled "Draft Amendments to the Income Tax Act" claiming that time had not permitted him to introduce these amendments during the debate on Bill C-139. This was his assertion when the Bill had been before the House for over three months, since December 7, 1981. It was another breakdown in the budgetary process. The amendments to the Income Tax Act consequent upon certain provisions of earlier budgets had been before Parliament for three and a half months and had only just been passed. Lo, a new set of proposed amendments was made public during a parliamentary recess. That document reached my desk on April 6 while I was in my riding during Easter recess. Is it any wonder that we ask ourselves where our Parliament is heading?
But that is still not the end of the story. We now come to the events of April 18 and 19 last. Those irregularities have been gone over at some length in the House and by the media, and the Chair has ruled that they do not constitute a breach of privilege. Breach of privilege or not-and I insist on my right as a Member of Parliament to remain unconvinced by the argumentation used to uphold the Minister of Finance-the events surrounding that occurrence of the zoom lens and the Minister of Finance's recovery proposals remain one of the sadder happenings of this overextended first session of this Thirty-second Parliament, which is now over 36 months old and going into its fourth year.
The Minister even had to compound his arrogant disregard for Parliament. The nature of his offence, though it may not have been regarded by the Speaker as a breach of privilege, was outlined by my colleague the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) on April 21, the first opportunity he had really to speak after seeing the material on the budget that had been tabled two evenings before on April 19. The account of the tabling of the various documents during and just following the presentation is provided by the Speaker in her ruling. There were so many documents involved, however, that it is difficult to extract from the Speaker's comments the exact documents or tables to which reference is made.
I know for a fact that I received one correcting document that very evening in the lobby. It was called an "addendum" and was intended as an insert after paragraph one on page three of the budget speech. It was in effect the Minister's apologia. It was not his recitation of mea culpa or meum delictum, his self-redeeming rationalization and the discovery of $200 million to add to the year's expenditures on recovery, but his own recovery.
I also received, upon request to the Table, as the Hon. Member for York-Peel was spelling out his question of privilege, a much more complete set of corrections to a number of

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Donald W. Munro
pages of a budget document entitled "Fiscal Plan". These corrections were in manuscript. It is a disgraceful looking document, one that ought not to have been tabled even to save the Minister's face and his skin. I am glad to say that document was not stamped by the Table. We have not only the "addendum" to the budget speech but also "the unrevised version" and the "hand-corrected version" of these budget papers. The confusion that these documents caused on their own, merited something more than the big, self-satisfied grin with which the Minister favoured us once he had been excused for his outrageous behaviour. It is worth noting the dates that I have already mentioned of these outrageous events.
Then on April 26 we had the ruling of the Speaker that there was no question of privilege. Surely there is a lesson to be drawn from this whole experience.
Given this history of shifts and changes, budget presentation and budget alterations-90 of them remember in one budget- and given that record of reversals and revisions, how can we be sure that the income tax provisions as they now stand, even for 1982-83 will remain intact? And because of that uncertainty, how are corporations in particular, and individuals to a lesser degree, to plan their financial future?
A stable tax climate, accent on stability, is all-important for healthy economic growth in the nation. That stability we have not had in Canada for at least four years now. Uncertainty and the burdensome national debt load, I suggest, are two of the principal obstacles to economic resurgence in Canada.
A word of caution therefore. Before we get out into the streets to sing the praises of this budget, let us think on these things. Let us dwell on the atmosphere of uncertainty that has been generated, and let us remember with respect to the debt load, to quote the lead editorial of the Financial Times of April 25, 1983:
The legacy of the past eight years is a collapse of federal revenues from 18.7 per cent of GNP in 1974-1975 to 15.7 per cent last year and a jump in expenditures from 19.9 per cent to 23.1 per cent.
This jump in expenditures is over the same period. A sobering summary, especially when coupled with the prospect of having to deal shortly with another borrowing Bill, this time for $19 billion. This will be on top of the $62.6 billion-let me repeat, on top of the $62.6 billion-already authorized during the life of this session of Parliament.
Having said all that, I am still at a bit of a loss, I must admit, to determine whether this whole budgetary fiasco in the Thirty-second Parliament can be laid at the door of carelessness or whether there may not be a deliberate scheme to downgrade the entire parliamentary process. In any event, the warning is worth sounding: once we are completely enmeshed in these devious toils, there will be no escape. Let us, therefore, be perpetually vigilant, lest we lose this instrument of democracy that has been so long in the making.
That being said, I would like to turn to another review of this Government's performance, but I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are rising.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I regret to interrupt but the Hon. Member's time has expired. He may continue with the unanimous consent of the House. There does not appear to be unanimous consent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro). The Hon. Member was in the House when I raised the question, which I think is vital in terms of the economic direction in which the country is going, with the Minister in charge of Small Business.
In reviewing the budget and looking at the economic conditions of the country, particularly as they apply to unemployment and even more particularly as they apply to single industry towns and older cities where municipalities have come to rely on established companies for their employment opportunities, does the Hon. Member have any comment to make on the proposal that we have reached a point where corporate decision making is not just simply the responsibility of the directors or for that matter the shareholders of each and every private corporation, that in order to develop a sense of responsibility to the municipality from which corporations derive significant benefit in terms of the infrastructure that is paid for by the citizens of the municipality-the roads, the sewers and the other things that go into making municipalities places where workers work and live-workers and their families who at times are totally ignored by decisions made to close plants- and I am sure that in the area the Hon. Member represents and from his past experience he has seen-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. The Hon. Member will have an opportunity to participate in the debate; therefore, would he put his question to the Hon. Member?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate what you are saying, but the rule says that I may ask a question or make a brief comment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: "Brief'.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is fine. Would the Hon. Member support a new code of corporate conduct that would require some prior consultation with those who are most affected in order that some solutions might be found to eliminate the need to close some of the plants that are being closed in this country and thus establish some stability in many municipalities?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an approach that is very similar to the approach being offered by the Government. What the Hon. Member fails to see is that within the taxation climate with which we are compelled to live, corporations are facing difficulties, grave difficulties. They are quite capable of managing their affairs, carrying on their business, and producing and employing if the tax structure allows them; but this proposal that came across the floor this morning, for example, is just another foot in the door for the socialist horde, if you like: "Let me get a hold of some of the equity of your company, and once we get in, we will take it over".
May 2, 1983

There is another solution, the solution of tax incentives, tax incentives to employ, to produce and to export. Those are the solutions which give the man who has the initiative pride in his work to expand.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Socialism has not worked. It cannot work. The other solution is the only one.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member just out of curiosity. If the tax incentive method is the one the Hon. Member is proposing, how does he rationalize it with a budget deficit that must grow as a result of reductions in taxes and as a result of tax incentives? How does he rationalize those two points?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is socialist economics if we ever heard it. The Hon. Member does not seem to realize that with increasing production and increasing employment there will be increasing taxes. It is as simple as that. The socialist approach has been tried in the country by this Government for over 15 years. The Hon. Member is able to talk about corporate responsibility and use that term without blushing. I am suggesting that corporate responsibility is what the Conservative philosophy engenders, encourages and rewards.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a short question to the Hon. Member. He says that the socialist approach is the one being used in the budget. Why is it, then, that commentators are calling it a Conservative budget and the stock market has kind of gone ape over it? The index has gone up and so on. Also he used the term "socialist hordes". Does he think the socialist hordes are at the gates of the Government of British Columbia?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We hope they stay outside.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, I think so. I recommend to the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) the April 25 edition of the Financial Times from which I drew some comments. All the media are not commenting favourably on the budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Ninety-eight per cent are.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the Hon. Minister wants to go by the 98 percentage, there are other percentages which I could bring to the attention of the House. For example, the drawdown of the earnings of Canadians is a very high percentage with which we should deal. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway should not get out on the streets and laud this Budget too highly, because he will come down with a bump one of these days.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having just heard from the far right of the House and also from the far left of the House, I would like to say a few
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
words on behalf of the common, practical, middle group in the House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let us take a look at the budget and its reality. I, like many other members in the House, have been here for some time and have seen many budgets brought in. We have always witnessed the same procedures prior to budgets, with Hon. Members rising and asking the Minister of Finance questions about what will be in them. When the Minister does not tell them, he is accused of being too secretive; when something happens, he is accused of a leak. Even when it is taken out of his office he is accused of a leak. Following the presentation of a budget, our mail load either lightens or strengthens according to what is in the budget. Of all the budgets I have seen going through the House, my mail load is the lightest it has ever been on any budget in the last 17 years. This is a clear indication that many people out there are satisfied with it and are willing to give it an honest and fair trial period.
I will talk about a number of matters this morning. One relates to a question which I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in the House a few days ago about the policies of Canadian chartered banks. I do not want my comments to be portrayed as bank beating. I think it is a problem which must be solved if we are to improve the unemployment situation in Canada. I am referring to the matter of projects financing of small businesses and small industry.
The chartered banks of Canada have lately had policies whereby they will not release funds to small industries to help them pay their labour or buy material so that they can produce manufactured goods, fill contracts and orders. As a result, I know of one company which recently had to turn down a $3 million contract. I want to make it very clear that there is very little sense in the Government putting up billions of dollars in an attempt to promote employment and asking members of the private sector to put their money on the line to try to improve the economy and the unemployment situation, if we do not have the total co-operation of the Canadian financial structure. I hope the Minister of Finance continues his discussions with the Canadian banking community so that small industries can get on with the job of producing goods, paying labour and creating more jobs.
In answer to my question the Minister of Finance indicated that he expected all sectors of the economy to carry their weight. That is the answer to the problem at which I am looking.
I was glad to see in the budget the Extended Youth Training and Employment Program whereby 5,000 young people will be taken into the Canadian Armed Forces to be trained in basic and general trades. The sum of $75 million will be allocated toward this Program. It will also provide vocational training. It will help young people make the transition from school eventually into the work force with trades and vocational training to

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
their credit. The Canadian Armed Forces has some very good instructors in the fields in which these young people will be studying. I want to tell the military community how much we appreciate the way they welcomed the Program with open arms. 1 am sure that they will do an excellent job.
I would like to refer to another area of activity which is a relatively untapped resource in the over-all structure of the Canadian economy. I am referring to the tourist industry. Over the years the Provinces have really not had an aggressive policy to develop or assist tourism. Of course, the federal Government is limited by jurisdiction, but I would like to give an example of an entrepreneurial effort that deserves a lot of credit. It is an area of the economy by which we can increase jobs and the tax flow into the treasury of Canada by helping others and providing them with a framework within which to work.
There is a great future in tourism. A case in point is the white water rafting business which operates on the Upper Ottawa River in the Beachburg-Forester's Falls area. Three companies have been playing a lead role in the development of white water rafting on the Upper Ottawa. Last year Wilderness Tours took 32,000 people down the white waters of the Ottawa River. Another company known as Ottawa River White Water Rafting brought down about 12,000 people. Another company, the OWL, Ottawa white water leaders, took down 5,000 people in 1982. In 1983 Wilderness Tours in particular is expected to go from the 32,000 in 1982 to 47,000. That is entrepreneurialship of the first order. This is why I wanted to put it on the record today.
I think both Governments, provincial and federal, must place a great deal more emphasis upon tourism because there is great future job potential. It is not an area which will be totally invaded by technology like industrial jobs. We could provide more jobs for general labour through the tourist industry than through any other existing industry at the present time.
These companies place a great emphasis upon safety. They have outstanding records in terms of safe operations. It is in their best interests for customers to have the benefit of good equipment and expert employees. These employees are well trained and the people who go on white water tours are in safe hands. To date they have not had an accident. This is a relatively new industry in Canada, approximately 12 years old. It is catching on fast and has great potential. The employment potential is outstanding.
There is something the Government must look at and do something about. Companies in the white water rafting business want safety regulations set by Government. This is not to protect their image, which they look after themselves. They want to be protected against others coming in with cheaper equipment which is not safe. This could cause accidents and give the whole industry a bad name.
I have been working with the Coast Guard people in the Department of Transport and with other levels of Government
to try and bring this about. The industry will be submitting regulations for our perusal and, hopefully, adoption. That is the route to go. Those in the industry are the experts. Regulations they submit will protect their interests and the safety of people. They know best. This is a good example where industry can work hand in hand with Government, bringing in regulations which will protect an important segment of the tourist industry in Canada.
I will retract a bit to point out that there is no Act of Parliament dealing with tourism safety, something that is needed. I hope we will see something along this line in the Throne Speech. At present, responsibility for regulations governing the safety of this industry is under, of all things, the Canada Shipping Act. Under the regulations of that Act, operators on the Fraser River in British Columbia are covered. There are general regulations which affect all operators, whether they be on B.C. rivers or on the Ottawa River between Ontario and Quebec.
There is need for a second set of regulations which are more technical. Obviously the equipment required on the Fraser River is different from that required on the Ottawa River. There should be two phases of regulations, a section of which should be more technical, related to the geography of an area such as that in which the white water rafters operate.
I wish to add to my argument with regard to how important that industry is to tourism. A large complex is to be built in Ross Township on the Ottawa River. The company building it, Wilderness Tours, will put up $800,000 of its own money. That is how much faith they have in the industry. They have received $110,000 in 50-50 federal-provincial funding from the Eastern Ontario subsidiary agreement. By next year, Wilderness Tours expect to have over 200 employees. That is a sizeable number and shows the employment potential.
Before my time runs out, I also want to deal with airports. Airports have been referred to in some of the follow-up documentation of the capital projects listed in the budget. I want to emphasize this very strongly. I hope the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and other Cabinet Ministers will take note of this point. Regional airports are very important. Some emphasis must be placed on capital funding for small regional airports. It is part of the infrastructure of those communities. You can try to attract industry, jobs, small and large businesses, but without proper facilities to provide the rapid transit which people demand you will not have the infrastructure which appeals to business leaders.
There are regional airports in Kapuskasing, Cochrane and other parts of Ontario. Pembroke is a case in point. The airport is owned by 12 municipalities. There are two return flights to Toronto a day. These small airports are important because they are feeder lines for the larger airlines. People can get where they want to go. These airports can handle private aircraft, both pleasure and business. Such an airport is an attraction for business.
There is little sense in Government spending millions of dollars on industrial parks and other infrastructure without
May 2, 1983

providing the total package. We must never forget the transportation factor. Any member of the northern Ontario caucus knows how important the transportation factor is. Flying schools are also very important. Many of these smaller airports provide such instruction. I repeat, these airports attract business to the area.
I do not want to conclude before saying something about forestry. As Hon. Members are aware, the northern Ontario caucus sponsored a forestry conference in Thunder Bay the first weekend in February. It was a major success. Business people from the various sectors of the industry across northern Ontario attended that conference. It provided good input. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts), to whom the Canadian Forestry Service reports, attended that conference, as did three or four other Cabinet ministers. I thank them. It is that type of interest and personal relationship that builds up confidence in the business community. Business people realize that the Government is interested in them. This is important if we want their help in improving the economy and, therefore, the employment situation in Canada.
At that conference we discussed basic issues involving the forest industry, including tax problems. I know there are special tax measures in the budget for those in the forestry business. There is something crucial in the future for the forest industry.
Those with a basic knowledge of the business realize that one of the major problems over the last number of years has been a lack of forest management. The federal Government is inhibited to a large degree with regard to upgrading our forests because of the jurisdictional problems. I have a note here which is rather revealing. It is headlined "Ownership". Approximately 92 per cent of Canadian forest lands, excluding the Yukon and Northwest Territories, is owned by the Provinces. Seven per cent is privately owned and less than 1 per cent is federal Crown land. That shows how inhibited the federal Government is without built-in federal-provincial agreements to upgrade the forests and put people to work in the forests.
Private ownership in the forest industry is significant in some parts of the Atlantic Provinces, the southern agricultural regions of Ontario and Quebec and in some of the prime forest areas of the B.C. coast. Domestic ownership of the pulp and paper industry was 70 per cent in 1980 and domestic ownership of sawmills and other wood industries was over 80 per cent. Approximately 75 per cent of Canada's combined forest products industries are domestically owned.
While the forestry sector is of obvious value to Canadians, employing over 11 per cent of our work force when in full production, several key variables present a challenge to the industry's continued strength. These include export trade, timber supply and general economic trends. It behooves us as a federal Government to keep in place tax measures that will be an incentive to the industry through difficult times and through good times as well so that a balance can be struck that will keep the industry intact. The forestry sector plays a major
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
role in upgrading the forests in our land. I cannot emphasize the importance of research and development in the forestry field strongly enough.
We must come to grips with the jurisdictional problem in Canada at the federal-provincial level so that the federal Government will be legally able to have greater input into reforestation programs and into improving Canada's forest species, as we now have a situation where there is far too much second and third grade timber. Many operators who have been in the business for years find this a real danger to their future. If there is anything that discourages them from expanding and creating more employment in those areas, it is the poor quality of timber.
Since the Minister of the Environment is here today, I would like to see this particular jurisdictional issue dealing with the forest industry of Canada go to a full-scale federal-provincial conference with forest resource Ministers from the various Provinces and appropriate Ministers from the federal Cabinet involved.
