I would like to see them come to a sound agreement so that there will be no more jockeying back and forth saying: "You cannot come into my backyard and I do not want you bringing in this money because you are interfering in my jurisdiction," and so on. If we are to have a mature forest, we must act like mature people and develop a good, sound program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise a related matter with the Hon. Member. I share his concern about the shortage of fibre which at one point appeared to be reaching crisis proportions in certain parts of Canada. However, because of a serious decline in sales of forest products, the fibre shortage problem at the moment seems to be taking second place to the more serious problem of how the forest products industry can sell their products. The industry has been exceedingly dependent upon the U.S. market, a market that has been very soft as of late. The result in Canada has been very high unemployment in that sector of our economy.
I would ask the Hon. Member if he has made any assessment of other possible markets that the forest industry could look to, and is he satisfied that the Government of Canada is doing all within its power to assist the industry in opening up those markets? If he has thought about this, what areas other than the U.S. market are areas the forest industry could look to with some optimism?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a very good question. The Hon. Member has noted that because of the downturn in the forest industry, there has not been the same demand for forest products. As a result, there is no longer a fibre shortage. That is my understanding of his statement. However, I would have to state that that is a poor way to improve the fibre shortage problem in Canada. I would hope that we would be able to bring in a program that, as I mentioned to the Minister of the Environment, will continue to improve and increase the wood fibre industry in Canada so that we can gear it to a strong economy and fibre will be in supply on a constant basis rather than only during future downturns in the economy.
As for trade, it is rather interesting that the Hon. Member should ask that question as I recently asked the Minister of Industry (Mr. Lumley) who is also the Minister in charge of DREE, a similar question in the Finance Committee. He informed me that his Department, prior to his taking on new duties, and when he was Trade Minister, worked in the Middle East and other areas of the world in an attempt to create more markets for Canadian wood products. I believe he mentioned a program that he recently initiated with the B.C. Government, the federal Government and the forest industry of B.C., each one paying a third of the cost to promote international sales. I believe that program is still ongoing. If the industry is willing to participate in that program, it will be of benefit to the program itself because the industry will want to see a very
aggressive policy of searching for markets for their business. I think the fact that they are part of the act will probably cause them to spur on Canadian Trade commissioners and others involved in the process. This is necessary, Mr. Speaker.
The recent problem we have gone through, safely for the time being, with the United States market is one that we do not want to see again for a long time. As the Hon. Member noted, it is a warning that we cannot rely forever and a day on the traditional markets but will have to go out and dig for new markets. Obviously the Middle East has to be one of the areas and the more emphasis we place on this, the better. Because the Hon. Member has raised the question and others have shown an interest in it, I think it would be interesting for Members of the House to receive the official update on where the program stands. We must review our sales programs from time to time in order to make sure that they are working well and that they are producing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had been looking forward with some degree of anticipation to the budget. As a result of some of the questions asked by Members of this Party and the answers received, I had come to believe that it is entirely possible that the Liberal Government had at last begun to understand the real problems of the land. I hoped that for the first time in the three years that I have been in this House it would acknowledge that unemployment was a matter of considerable seriousness, and that the majority of the unemployed were faced with severe economic dislocation that could affect many of them permanently. I had hoped that the Government was going to address that particular problem directly as a priority.
I confess to a sense of disappointment on budget night. I listened with interest; in fact, I was rigidly fixed as I watched the Minister go through his budget. I waited, as did many Canadians, at least two million and maybe more, for that point in the budget statement where he would begin to speak about their problems.
Many of these people have worked in factories and offices for 25, 30 or 35 years. They have gone to work every day, doing what they were asked, producing what was required of them. For this they received a remuneration that allowed them to live at an average level and perhaps buy a home some years ago and raise their families. Now they are unemployed at an age when finding an alternative occupation is extremely difficult, if not impossible for some of them. They are unemployed at a time when they were looking forward to building a nest egg for their retirement, at a time when unemployment means a cessation of contributions to the pension plan to which they belong. In the final analysis, that means their pension will be less when they reach age 65 or whatever is retirement age in their occupation. They are people between the ages of 54 and 62 primarily who look to us for some sense of how their problems can be resolved.
May 2, 1983

The budget did not even recognize that was happening. Neither did the budget recognize that there are literally tens of thousands of young people, some in the 20 to 30 age group, recently married with families to raise and pretty bleak job prospects. There are others who are leaving institutions of higher learning, university or post-secondary schools, who do not know where to look for the employment that we have long said was the desire of this society.
A week ago today, at just about this time of day, I spoke in Hamilton to 300 high school students. They asked me, quite justifiably, what kind of employment opportunities there are for them. They are not able to go on to post-secondary education, nor do they see the benefit of it. Where are the jobs that successive Governments have led them to believe would be available for them? They are willing and eager to work but they do not know where to turn. In many instances their parents are unemployed, so they know that if they are unable to find employment with the experience they have, their own chances are severely reduced. They asked what is going to happen to the country and where it is going.
Why did this come about, Mr. Speaker? It is all too easy to suggest that current economic conditions are the result of decisions made or economic downturns that occurred in other parts of the world. That is a cop out. Of course we were affected by the world downturn, but we did little if anything to try to compensate for that by improving and increasing economic activity in Canada. We took the view that we- meaning the Government, and I might go so far as to say the Conservatives-were not required to support the kind of measures proposed by this Party two years ago when it was evident what we were about to face. They were not prepared to support the kinds of measures that would have resulted in job creation in the municipalities across the country that even then were beginning to show an economic downturn.
When we were talking about building the railroad and providing job opportunities and a decent transportation system for Canada, the Tories and Liberals said it could not be done and that we could not afford it. When we were talking about building homes to accommodate those who could not find a decent place to live at a price they could afford, it was the Tories and the Liberals who said we could not afford it.
When we were saying we ought to be going ahead with the completion of the east-west pipeline in order that we could be truly energy self-sufficient and at the same time create jobs and build an infrastructure that would enable the country to grow, it was the Tories and the Liberals who said we could not afford it. They said that when there were 900,000 people unemployed and the deficit was $11 billion. That is when they said we could not afford it. Now we have two million people unemployed, the deficit will be over $30 billion, and, more important, we are spending about $1 billion per day to keep people unemployed.
When we look at that we must say there was gross mismanagement based upon the Conservative-based policy of fiscal abuse and an inability to understand that investment in Canadians is good investment. The Tories and the Liberals said that we could not afford it.
I will come back to that after one o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

Madam Speaker, despite the current recession, agriculture continues to be one of the strongest contributors to our economy. Consequently one would expect that the commitment to agricultural research and development, which is so essential to the future
viability of this sector, would be uppermost in any wellmeaning Minister's mind. However, agricultural research does not seem to fit within the hierarchy of the Liberal Cabinet's priorities.
Over the past decade the annual increase of Agriculture Canada expenditures on agricultural research and development represented about 1 per cent. This lack of growth in spending on research has meant that our country has fallen behind in terms of adequate facilities, equipment, and research staff. If nothing else, this should make the Liberal Cabinet think twice when it considers further reductions in research investment.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the CRTC's telecom decision on hearing aid compatibility of telephones, granted residential and business telephone subscribers the right to buy their telephones from any manufacturer, but did not require that the newly purchased phones have the same "fluxcoil" contained in the Bell Canada phones, which allows them to be used by any hearing aid wearers.
The pending proliferation of incompatible phones will require the 200,000 hearing aid wearers to buy and carry around a battery-powered, hockey puck shaped, acoustic coupler and hold it between telephone handsets and their hearing aids. subtopic: CHANGE SOUGHT OF CRTC TELEPHONE EQUIPMENT DECISION
CHANGE SOUGHT OF CRTC TELEPHONE EQUIPMENT DECISION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last November the CRTC decided not to require that all telephones meet a technical standard which would ensure that telephones would be compatible with the use of hearing aids. By making this decision, the CRTC missed a golden opportunity to demonstrate leadership in the telecommunications field and to advance the human rights of hearing impaired Canadians.
Telephone accessibility is a vital issue for Canada's 1.5 million hearing impaired citizens. The CRTC's decision will have a profound effect on employment opportunities for the hearing impaired, and on their ability to have contact with family and friends, as well as their ability to communicate within the community generally. To the hearing impaired it also means a frustration of their right to live independently.
The Canadian-Co-ordinating Council on Deafness, the Canadian Hard of Hearing Association, the Canadian Hearing Society, and the Hard of Hearing Club of Ottawa have requested, through a petition to the Cabinet, that the CRTC decision be changed. In all of these circumstances it is inappropriate, and not in accordance with acceptable public policy, to allow this obstacle to be placed before the right of the hearing impaired to equal, universal use of the telephone system.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):

subsubtopic: CENTRAL AMERICA-REPRESENTATIONS MADE TO UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. A week ago he said that there were, in his view, major differences between the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States concerning policies affecting Latin America. Specifically, he said:
We object to the interference in the internal affairs of other countries by any major power, even if that power is a friend.
Considering that since the Prime Minister made that statement the President of the United States has said that his Government intends to continue financing and training groups who will be making invasions into Nicaragua from Honduras, does the Prime Minister stand by what he said just over a week ago? Did he make that clear to the President of the United States?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: CENTRAL AMERICA-REPRESENTATIONS MADE TO UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext: Yes, Madam Speaker, I do. What I indicated clearly to the President of the United States is that I thought he had made a very positive suggestion when he proposed in his statement to Congress that there be an agreement by all parties, an international verifiable agreement, that neither side-the U.S., Soviet Union, Cuba nor any other power in this case-intervene in the internal affairs of the Central American States. I thought that was a very positive suggestion. I hope it would have the support from my hon. friend.

subsubtopic: CENTRAL AMERICA-REPRESENTATIONS MADE TO UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext: I am pleased to indicate to the Prime Minister that that kind of proposal has our unequivocal support. We have said that a number of times.

subtopic: TRAINING OF INSURGENTS BY UNITED STATES
TRAINING OF INSURGENTS BY UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the President's address to Congress which seemed to be aimed very clearly at getting additional funds for military related activities in that region, he also said that the reason the United States was financing and training groups in Honduras that were making attacks in Nicaragua was to prevent the flow of arms from Nicaragua to El Salvador. Since then, just yesterday in fact, the head of the largest insurgent group that has been financed and trained by the United States, denied the truth of what President Reagan said. He said in fact that the groups have nothing to do with stopping the flow of arms to El
Salvador but that their main purpose is "ousting the present government in Nicaragua".
Considering tht the insurgent groups themselves are saying that, will the Prime Minister follow up on his earlier criticism of such activity by indicating to the United States that the Government of Canada disapproves of this kind of interference that is being encouraged by the United States, and that costs lives?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRAINING OF INSURGENTS BY UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I made it clear to my interlocutors that, as far as the objectives and historical analysis of the events in Central America were concerned, Canada was not in agreement with the United States, and I know that my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, also made that point to Secretary Shultz.
With respect to the point of non interference by outside powers in that area, I am very happy to hear that the NDP has stated, and I quote its Leader, "The President of the United States has unequivocal support of the NDP on that point". I think it is important to put that on the record because very often the Leader of the NDP makes light of my support for the President of the United States. I think he should be thanked now for having made it clear that he also unequivocally supports the President of the United States on that point.

Madam Speaker, it seems to me that the fact that lives are being lost every day in that region merits a little more concern than scoring what seems to be rather trivial debating points. I indicated our clear support for that part of the statement of the President of the United States where he called for a treaty among all states involved in the region that would be verifiable and would prohibit interference in other States' activities. I also mentioned that the Government of Nicaragua has long indicated support for that.
I come back to my question to the Prime Minister. Will he now make his position clear that the United States activity in financing and training groups-the head of which in the past 24 hours, said that their purpose is to bring down the Government of Nicaragua-must stop, and the Canadian Government takes an unequivocal position on it?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am just as unequivocal as the Hon. Member when I condemn the interference by other countries in the affairs of Central American countries, just as I condemned certain countries in the area for their interference in countries of that area. I think I had the support of the President of the United States when I re-enunciated my expression of Canadian Government policy that what happens in a country is its own affair. When a country begins to export its revolution to other countries then we begin to worry.
May 2, 1983

The reason I underscored the support of the Leader of the New Democratic Party for the President's policy is not to make a trivial debating point. It is because so often the Leader of the NDP, because we support the Americans in some things, assumes that we support them in all things and that in some way we are in a position of solidarity with their position on Central America. Just as with the NDP, there are some things that we think the United States does well and some things on which we do not support them. My answer was making that quite clear. I am glad I am sharing the same ground as the Leader of the NDP on this.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of National defence. Then, at that time, we had a reduction in man-years from the previous year for term employees. Therefore, we had to lay off many of them. Then came the NEED Program which gave us some money and supplementary man-years to hire some people under certain conditions. subsubtopic: DEDUCTIONS FOR CHILD CARE EXPENSES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. It concerns the inequities in the income tax policy concerning the child care expense deduction. It is our understanding that in order to qualify for the $2,000 per child tax deduction for child care expenses both parents must be working, unless the lower income spouse is infirm, in an institution, or is a full-time student. Will the Minister agree that this policy discriminates against thousands of unemployed parents who are in a situation quite frequently these days where a father or mother is laid off but he or she must have child care in order to seek employment? Such a family is not eligible to deduct child care
May 2, 1983

costs nor are the increasing numbers of low-income families who pay little or no income tax. What will he do about these inequities?

subsubtopic: DEDUCTIONS FOR CHILD CARE EXPENSES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have indicated that people who are unemployed and are searching for jobs are obviously in situations where they do not have jobs. This is a situation similar to other cases under the Income Tax Act where some benefits are available only to those in a particular situation. In this case the requirement is that one has to have child care expenses because one is not at home to look after children.
The fact is that most people who are unemployed find work during the course of the year. If we look at the statistics we see this. There is no doubt about it. In order to claim the total Child Tax Credit one does not need to have a high income during the course of the year. For example, a family with two children will be able to claim the full $4,000 child care expense if the lower income earner makes $6,000 in the year. This example demonstrates the accessibility of this particular program and the relative ease with which one can benefit from it.

subsubtopic: DEDUCTIONS FOR CHILD CARE EXPENSES
speechtext: My understanding of the figures is that one out of five unemployed people is unemployed over a year and certainly would be paying very little income tax, and therefore would not be eligible for this benefit.

REQUEST THAT TAX CREDIT REPLACE CURRENT PROVISION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we believe that all families, regardless of income, must have access to affordable quality daycare. It would not cost any more but it would provide the greatest benefits to those with the greatest needs. How about that?

However, it is not the responsibility of the federal Government to assume the administration of daycare centres in the country. It is a provincial responsibility.

Member's suggestion is concerned, I remind her that in the budget I have maintained the Child Tax Credit at a higher level than would have been otherwise, exactly for the reasons referred to by the Hon. PROCESSING OF CLAIMS FOR REFUGEE STATUS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. He knows there has been great concern expressed by Members of the House with respect to the time required for the processing of claims for refugee status under the Immigration Act. Can the Minister tell the House how he will deal with the problem, and when?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: PROCESSING OF CLAIMS FOR REFUGEE STATUS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should point out to Hon. Members of the House that, because of the increasing incidents of difficulty in other parts of the world, the number of refugee claims in Canada went up in 1982 to over 3,500. Obviously that has put a very severe strain on the system that was elaborated under the Immigration Act, 1978, particularly the one requiring that there be a series of appeals from the Refugee Advisory Committee to the Appeal Board. In order to speed up that system substantially we are starting today two major projects-one in Toronto and one in Montreal, the two international centres-in which oral hearings will be allowed in front of the Refugee Advisory Committee. This will substantially increase both the fairness and, we hope, the speed.
Our estimate is that we should be able to speed up the processing by close to a year and therefore make a substantial inroad into the backlog which has developed because of the enormous volume of refugee claims we are now receiving.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister responsible for the Post Office. It is a question about big versus small. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was in the midst of putting on the record my views with regard to the complicity between the Tories on the one hand and the Liberal Party on the other hand in an attempt to deprive Canadians of an opportunity to work.
I know that there are in this country a large number of people who, when the budget was presented slightly less than a week ago, were very disappointed. They had hoped to be able to see some signs that the budget would bring about the economic recovery which would ultimately put them back to work. They had also hoped, in the area which I represent, to see some indication on the part of the Government that it understood the destruction which was taking place in some of the older municipalities in Canada as a result of decisions being made by companies, some of long standing, to close their doors and to walk away. Some were leaving to go to other municipalities, maybe because they were being offered additional incentives. Some were rationalizing their enterprises, as they like to put it, in order to maximize profits. Others were moving from Canada altogether, some to the United States, to allow their home base manufacturing operation to have more
May 2, 1983

of the North American market production, and others still were moving offshore altogether.
Last week, in a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and in a subsequent question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley), 1 suggested that it was time that we in Canada began to understand the devastation created by the unilateral moves being made by these companies. 1 suggested that it was time for us to demand some quite different corporate behaviour and that it is necessary for the decision-makers in the corporate sector to recognize the investment which municipalities have laid out in providing the necessary infrastructure which made it possible for them to locate there in the first place. It is time for those same corporate decision makers to understand the destructive nature of their decisions as they relate to workers and their families and the problems which occur when the main breadwinner, be it a male or a female, is suddenly found no longer to have employment. Often this happens to them at an age when finding alternative employment is virtually impossible.
Today, when the Minister in charge of small businesses was speaking in the debate, I asked him whether he did not think it was time that the Government presented to the House of Commons some measure on behalf of the people of Canada to try to come to grips with the destruction which has now become a part of all too many communities in every part of the country.
Let me just tell Hon. Members about Hamilton. In the last two weeks, we have heard three major announcements involving companies of some long standing. In two cases, the companies were closing entirely. In another case, the company was laying off its entire work force, with no real date for return in sight. We were speaking of hundreds of people who had put out everything they had on behalf of those companies. In no instance was there prior consultation or opportunity for the employees, their representatives, the municipality representing the taxpayers in Hamilton, the provincial Government representing a substantial investment in our municipality or the federal Government to meet with the companies involved to discuss an alternative.
After years in Hamilton, Consolidated Bathurst sent its employees a letter at Christmas last year thanking them for the hard work they had done which had resulted, in part, in the company having a substantially better year than it had had in many years. In fact, it was enjoying a profit. The letter stated, "We look forward to your cooperation next year in making 1983 an even better year". The company then sat down with those same employees and their representatives at the negotiating table in January and they reached a decision as to the contract. There was not one single hint that the plant was planning to close, not a whisper that it proposed to move out of the community altogether.
In March, not two months later, an announcement came out of the blue that the plant would be closed, the equipment would be sold and the production would be moved to the Montreal base. That is just not good enough. That kind of behaviour is obscene. It was a clear indication of a lack of
The Budget-Mr. Deans
corporate understanding. If it were one isolated case, one might say that this must certainly be considered, but over and against everything else, it is unusual. However, it is not an isolated case. Just last week we discovered that Allan Industries had decided not to reopen its plant. There was no one single hint that it proposed to close. There was no discussion, no opportunity to consider the possibility of assistance in finding markets. There was no opportunity to discuss whether assistance of one kind or another might enable it to create a more profitable position for itself and, therefore, for its employees. We discovered it was closing because a reporter from the Hamilton Spectator called to ask when the company expected to return to production. It was mentioned that the company had prepared a press release dated approximately two weeks previously, which it had not bothered releasing, indicating that the plant was to be closed and that the work was to be done in the parent plant in the United States.
Then, of course, International Harvester was once the mainstay of the Hamilton community, but we find that now it is in dire straits. What do we see? We see these workers accepting a vastly reduced contract arrangement but, even at that, there is still no work for them.
One goes through the municipality and finds that there are places where we could in fact have been creating employment directly. National Steel Car has an idle capacity of almost 100 per cent. The Government could and should be ordering its hopper cars but it has not yet placed its order, keeping those workers unemployed, making it less and less likely that the plant will return to full production. I am saying to Your Honour that there are examples after examples in my community of decisions to close which have detrimentally affected people and where the companies involved have not even had the common decency to discuss the matter in advance. On the other hand, companies which ought to be working at a much greater level of production, or even at all as in the case of National Steel Car, are being impeded by decisions that are either being made or not made by the Government.
The Government has brought forward a budget which states that if a company wishes to retool its operation to make it more productive, the Government will help. But that is not the problem in this country. There is up to 30 per cent or 35 per cent of unused productive capacity now. Who in his right mind who has a plant with 30 per cent of its capacity idle would borrow money to create an entirely new productive capacity far in excess of what he has now and have 50 per cent or 60 per cent of it sitting idle? That is not where the problem lies. The problem is at the consuming end where consumers have lost confidence in this Government. Consumers have lost confidence that the Government's measures will help them in any beneficial way.
Interestingly enough, the Government is supported right down the line by its Conservative allies at every single turn. When we proposed that there ought to be stronger measures to make it more profitable for consumers to purchase now and

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mr. LeBlanc
better measures to get plants into production now, all that we heard from both the Conservatives and the Liberals was that we cannot afford it.
We should not ask whether we can afford to embark upon the necessary projects in this country that will create work, establish a strong and viable infrastructure in order to transport our goods and have the port facilities capable of handling those goods, to make ourselves energy self-sufficient from coast to coast and be able to use our skilled industries properly. Rather, the question should be, can we afford not to do it? Our answer is clearly that we cannot afford not to embark on projects like that. They should be undertaken now so that people can be put to work instead of being paid to sit at home.

speakeroldname: Hon. Romlo LeBlanc (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support these measures I would first like to commend my colleague, the Minister of Finance, (Mr. Lalonde), for the imaginative approach to the economic challenges which face us. Many of the measures which he set out are meant to encourage Canadians to invest in their own industries, to facilitate the growth of our productive capacity and to create the type of climate in which productive enterprises will thrive.
The Minister of Finance has made it clear that the Government's first concern is to help those Canadians who want to work and cannot find jobs. That goal calls for what the Minister of Finance has described as a new partnership for recovery, involving labour, business and Government united by a sense of national purpose.
This is what this Government has done in housing. It has provided incentives and encouraged Canadians to purchase and repair their homes. In fact, the annual rate of starts has increased from 86,000 last summer to 177,000 in March. This improvement in housing starts translates directly into jobs. Given the estimates by the industry associations, these figures suggest that employment related to residential construction will increase from about 176,000 to approximately 354,000.
Yet that is not the full story. The Government's home renovation assistance has added a further 20,000 person-years of employment. These achievements clearly demonstrate the Government's concern for the unemployed.
We have taken a realistic course and one which will see jobs created. But it is a course that recognizes that any sustained growth must come from the private sector. This budget recognizes that no matter how well the private sector may operate as an engine of economic growth, there will be people who still need help to provide for themselves the necessities of life. In difficult times their lot is painful. I share my colleague's pride that this Government has not removed the social program protection for those who need help the most, especially for those who are not organized in order to negotiate from a position of strength.
I particularly welcome the measures which strenghthen our traditional social programs and make special provisions to assist low income families with the raising of children. The Government's commitment to economic recovery and job creation and its concern for those in greatest need apply equally in one of my areas of responsibility, which is housing. A total of $335 million in additional resources over the next 18 months has been allocated to housing in this budget. It is designated for the purpose of stimulating economic activity, creating jobs and extending assistance to those people, including native peoples, who are living in inadequate, crowded or unaffordable accommodation. This is in addition to over $1 billion that has been channelled into housing measures over the past year, over and above the regular CMHC budget of some $2 billion.
I welcome the decision to allocate another $30 million to the Canadian Home Ownership stimulation Plan because this extension will enable assistance to be available to small builders, in particular to those who could not start houses through difficult winter conditions. This new allocation will approach the figure of $750 million as the total Government investment in the home ownership plan, and that means that already more than 200,000 Canadian households have been assisted in buying a home.
The Minister of Finance also announced significant modifications to the Registered Home Onwership Savings Plan. These changes will encourage those who have invested in Registered Home Onwership Savings to use these savings to purchase a new home and furniture and appliances. It will continue the stimulus that has already been provided to the housing sector. It will encourage savings to be taken out of bank accounts and put to work creating employment, generating housing starts and demands for furniture and appliances.
This measure has been criticized as being inequitable and as offering greater benefits to the wealthy. Let me say that over 80 per cent of RHOSP contributors have incomes between $10,000 and $30,000. Less than 2 per cent have incomes over $50,000. First-time homebuyers are not wealthy.
As I said earlier, starts in March were at an annual rate of
177,000.	With the extension of the Home Ownership Stimulation Plan and the additional incentives provided through the changes that I have just described, we will have a good chance of exceeding the 150,000 starts predicted for 1983. I think we might go well beyond that mark if we can continue to instil confidence in the housing market, especially if there are no jumps in the interest rate situation that we have at present.
The housing industry associations have responded very favourably to these measures. The Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada has said that it is very happy with the budget and has predicted that these measures will increase housing starts by as much as 10,000. This means an additional 20,000 to 25,000 person-years of employment.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, besides, the Chairman of the Retail Council of Quebec stated that the changes in provisions with respect to furnishings and household appliances will provide a new stimulus for the purchase of expensive items which has been a major problem in the retail trade during the last eighteen months. The Director General of the Quebec Furniture Manufacturers' Association, an organization representing about 500 furniture
May 2, 1983

manufacturers, said that the Budget would make a big difference to them.
1 also would like to point out that the Government has not forgotten tenants. There has been an encouraging improvement in the vacancy rate recently, but there is still a shortage of rental accommodation in certain areas. 1 shall recall, if I may, that the Canada Rental Supply Plan introduced last year was, in fact, aimed at correcting local shortages. To date, some
14,000	rental units have benefited from this plan and 16,000 more may do so in 1983.
1 would like to add that our Home Ownership Stimulation Plan, by helping tenants to purchase a home, is helping to increase the number of housing units available. As I mentioned before, the Government has not forgotten its social responsibility. In the housing area, steps have been taken to implement programs that will help Canadians with low or modest incomes to improve their homes or to acquire one. These measures are also helping to create jobs. Some $325 million has been provided in the budget for helping low-or middle-income families through home renovation programs, non-profit housing programs, co-operative housing and Indian on-reserve housing.
Our housing stock is getting older. More and more attention will need to be paid to maintaining and improving the existing stock. Close to one million houses are in need of some major repair. The Government's decision to provide an additional $160 million for home renovation combines good housing policy, its concern with low and moderate income households, and job creation.
Of this $160 million, $120 million has been provided for the Canadian Home Renovation Plan. This has proved to be a popular and successful program. It is very effective in generating employment and stimulating economic activity since home owners are required to put up $3 of their own for every $1 of Government grant. By those terms, the additional $120 million announced by the Finance Minister will result in a total new investment of $480 million. The average income of households benefiting under this plan has been assessed at between $20,000 and $24,000.
A further $40 million has been allocated to the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, commonly known as RRAP. RRAP helps low income households maintain their homes in a safe, healthy and satisfying condition.
The RRAP Program is a sensitive Program, preserving both the housing stock and the social fabric of the community. In fact, one of my colleagues at an international conference said recently that under the Program houses are repaired with the use of the wheelbarrow and not the bulldozer.
I know all Members of this House will agree that our native people face housing conditions which are often unacceptable. This Government has provided a further $40 million for building and improving housing on Indian reserves. That pro-
77) e Budget-Mr. LeBlanc
gram is administered by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), but in terms of my own portfolio, I want to tell Hon. Members that funds for the rural and native housing program were recently increased by $6.7 million for 1983 and by $20 million for 1984 and succeeding years.
But the budget did not stop there, Mr. Speaker. The budget increased by 2,500 to 25,000 the number of units that will be supported this year under our social housing programs. This represents a commitment of some $125 million over the life of these projects.
It is easy to talk about these housing measures in terms of units and dollars and it is easy to speak about this in a somewhat impersonal way, but these measures affect real people, real households, in a direct way. They are not just dollars. They dramatically affect the well-being of low income households, be they in our cities, in our rural areas or on reserves. We are talking about programs which assist the elderly. Yesterday in my own riding I saw the opening of some 20 units for the elderly. These programs also assist the disabled. I recently saw a co-operative housing project which counted among its occupants a good number of handicapped people. These programs assist single parent families, victims of family violence, and our native peoples. There can be no doubt that this budget, while good for business, also addressed many pressing housing needs faced by low income Canadians.
During the year ahead, as in months past, housing will continue to play a vital part in putting more people to work, not just on the building sites but in all those sectors of business which produce building materials and supplies and which make and distribute the furnishings, appliances and household goods and services that people buy when they move into a new house. These materials, supplies, goods and services are mainly produced in Canada. Through housing, the Government has provided economic stimulation while at the same time rendering an essential social service by providing good, affordable shelter in a safe community environment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Hon. Member and I disagree on the issue; I think we may disagree on some of the wording. I take issue with him somewhat when he refers to social housing being limited to the 25,000 units, as important as they are. I might say that some SI60 million-and I would have to check the exact figure-is spent under RRAP which is really directed to low-income families. It provides forgivable loans and in many cases allows people in rural areas-and I have seen some in my own Province-to remain in their own homes and in fact continue to enjoy the milieu in which they have grown up and spent their adult lives. In a way this program is a social housing program as well.
The condition of the housing of native people certainly allows me to refer to the very considerable budget increased by $40 million by the Minister of Finance a few days ago. This is social housing of the highest priority. Because of the per unit cost of the program, in other words the cost of finding a housing solution for a relatively small number of people compared with the need, my predecessor ordered an evaluation of social housing programs. That evaluation is now in our hands. I hope it will be made available to Hon. Members who are interested in housing in the coming weeks or months so that we may have a discussion. Organizations including the co-operative housing movement recognize that we must find a way to bring in more people under social housing programs. As the Hon. Member indicated, the queue of people waiting is very long.
I do not want to return to the creation of ghettos. I do not think anyone in the House would want that. As I said a few days ago, we must find a way to get a bit more bang for the buck. I recognize this and I continue to impress it on my colleagues, but 1 think it will require a fair amount of imagination by all those concerned in the area of social programs to find a way, be it a rental allowance that has some pros and cons or some other, to accommodate more people who are waiting.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the presentation of the budget on April 19 many Hon. Members who have spoken in this debate have dealt with many of its varied aspects in very concrete ways. Therefore, in order not to be repetitive, I will direct my comments on this budget to two specific areas, agriculture and tourism. In real terms, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) gave only token assistance to these two sectors of the economy that today face serious difficulty. With regard to agriculture, the extra $100 million available in the budget is available only to farmers in distress. This is characterized by many producers as nothing more than a band-aid solution since in Ontario there are only 5,000 to
8,000	farmers who would qualify as being in dire straits.
With regard to the Finance Minister's announcement that he will allow farmers to carry their losses over ten years instead of seven, this too is not much more than a band-aid solution. If the Minister were inflicted with a serious physical wound. I am sure he would expect more than a band-aid, yet that is all he offers to the farmers in distress, many of whom are being forced to leave farms which their families have occupied for generations.
Members opposite have asked what our Party would do and what solutions we have for agriculture. First, our Party would provide up to $100 million to assist producers in re-negotiating their existing high interest loans to levels more in line with current rates. We would establish farm financial review boards which would be used as an advisory and appeal mechanism and would be set up in each Farm Credit Corporation region.
In addition, we would implement the agri-bond concept which would encourage retired farmers and others to invest their savings with the Farm Credit Corporation and thus provide tax incentives, including a waiver of capital gains tax.
The Budget-Mr. Mitges
This would pave the way for stable and low interest rates and a continuing source of available capital for agriculture. As this House knows, the agri-bond concept has wide support across the country, including the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
We also advocate the elimination of the 9 per cent federal sales tax on farm fuels. Although Canadian farmers use only 3 per cent of all energy consumed in Canada, they use 6 per cent of the gasoline and 10 per cent of the diesel fuel. About one-quarter of the farm operating expenses are owing to the direct and indirect cost of energy. The removal of the 9 per cent sales tax would reduce the cost of diesel fuel by 20 cents per gallon, and the elimination of a natural gax and gas liquids tax would result in reducing the price of natural gas and fertilizers, thereby lowering the general cost of farm operations. All these measures Canadian farmers would have welcomed from the Minister of Finance with, I dare say, open arms.
In today's desperate economic conditions, many farmers have been forced to engage in other off-farm activities to maintain a semblance of cash flow and to help maintain their farm operations. Therefore, we support repealing Section 31 of the Income Tax Act which is being used by Revenue Canada as a means of reclassifying such farmers as part-time farmers, thereby limiting farm loss to only $5,000. This reclassifying has resulted in many farmers being hit with back taxes in the thousands of dollars at a time when many such farmers are on the brink of financial collapse.
We strongly urge the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres), and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to take a long, hard look on what this section is doing to the agriculture industry. Indeed, because of the present Government's over-zealous enforcement of Section 31, many in the agricultural industry have the impression that the Government's secret goal is to replace the independent family farm with the large corporate farm.
I would be remiss if I did not mention tourism as far as this budget is concerned. There is a conspicuous absence of any concrete mention of tourism in this budget. Tourism is an industry that needs a lot of help and support, but it is not getting it from this Government. It gets lots of rhetoric, lip service, but no concrete assistance. This was well expressed by a constituent of mine, Mr. Gordon Canning, president of Blue Mountain Resorts Ltd. of Collingwood, Ontario, in a letter dated April 25, in which he said to me:
We are certainly having our problems as an industry in being recognized by the federal Government. The recent budget just reinforces our unhappiness and exasperations. In a brief to the Hon. Paul Cosgrove, Minister of State for Finance, the Tourism Industry Association of Canada asked simply for a recognition in the budget that tourism was of vital importance to Canada's economy. That recognition was not given and indeed the policies announced have a negative impact on the tourist industry or give support to other industries. For example, the tax on liquor has been increased-and although we can claim tax credits for certain kitchen equipment, other equipment such as snowmaking, grooming and chair-lift equipment did not apply because they are not used to produce goods for sale or lease. Prior to the last budget we were allowed full capital costs allowance in the first year on new investments, but that was reduced to half and no change was made to that ruling in last week's budget.

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Mitges
He went on to say that in helping to do its share, the provincial Government has already committed $12 million for municipal services in the Blue Mountain/Craig Leith area. The official plan for the development of the area, if it occurs, will involve over $100 million worth of construction.
The acceleration of this plan will depend on the federal-provincial tourist agreement that has been forthcoming for the last two and a half years. This is indeed a long time to discuss any agreement. In the meantime, everything is at a standstill just because some politicians and some bureaucrats cannot make up their minds. This is indeed a sad state of affairs.
The plight of the tourist industry in Canada was well documented in the debate that took place in the House of Commons on Thursday, April 13 of this year. Possible solutions were well documented. The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Rompkey) took part in the debate and seemed to be in accord with many of the recommendations made in the debate. It only remains to be seen what action will spring forth as the result. All of us hope, for the sake and for the survival of the tourist industry in Canada, that some long-awaited positive initiatives will be undertaken.
Although I stated that my comments will be mainly directed to agriculture and tourism as dealt with in the budget of the Minister of Finance, there are other areas of this budget that require a brief comment. For example, there is the bleak prospect for the unemployed to whom the Minister of Finance offered yet another band-aid. Today over two million Canadians are unemployed. Unemployed people want to work but cannot find jobs.
It is hard to take the Minister of Finance seriously when one considers that by March 31, 1983, only 32 per cent of the greatly-touted NEED Program was committed, never mind spent. Regardless of how you look at it, the bottom line of this Program is not really to get people back to permanent work but to help them re-qualify for UIC benefits. The unemployed want real and lasting jobs, not Government handouts. By and large this new budget does nothing to give the unemployed any real hope for bona fide jobs.
As for youth unemployment, this is indeed a national disaster. On budget night, the Finance Minister proudly announced an extra $70 million for this summer's student employment program. However, when one considers that in 1982 the program was cut from $120 million in 1981 to $100 million, this budget's $170 million program really represents only a $50 million increase from 1981.
The Minister of Finance is playing a numbers game regarding the 621,000 unemployed young Canadians under the age of 25. Perhaps what is even more serious is that this Government by its policies seems to be trying to create the idea among young Canadians and saying to them, "Don't worry, we'll find you a temporary Government-sponsored make-work job. When that runs out, we will give you unemployment insurance. When that runs out, we will introduce another Government program just long enough to requalify you for Unemployment Insurance benefits once again." I wonder
about the lasting effect that attitude will have on our country's future productivity levels and on the young people of Canada.
It should also be noted, Mr. Speaker, that despite the Finance Minister's glowing description of the employment programs, the true fact is that in 1984, there will be 55,000 fewer people with jobs than there were in 1981.
As we are all aware, a great concern of our Party is the financing of this budget. There is the old saying that there are two things a person cannot escape in this life, death and taxes. There is a third word that this administration will add to that old saying, and I will return to that in a moment.
To finance this recovery program, the Finance Minister announced that the 1982-1983 deficit will be about $25.3 billion and in 1983-1984 will be $31.3 billion. To help finance this so-called budget that is supposed to get business going and increase employment, he will increase the federal manufacturers' sales tax from 9 per cent to 10 per cent effective October 1, 1984. As this tax is imposed at the manufacturer's level, it will be a hidden tax. This also means that this increase will not filter down to the retail level until a few months later, in plenty of time for the 1984 election to have come and gone. In addition, this increase will probably be passed on to consumers who will likely blame the merchant, not the Government. How does the Minister of Finance expect to get business going in these economically precarious times with a policy of increasing the costs of business? How does he expect the embattled and cautious consumer to spend money when he raises the price of products?
I have never before heard of a policy that will get consumers to spend, make industries more productive and lower employment by increasing production costs and that is just what this tax increase does. In fact, this tax increase violates the main theme in the Minister of Finance's budget of getting the unemployed back to work.
The third word which the Minister of Finance has inserted into the old phrase is deficits. "All Canadians can look forward to death, deficits and increased taxes." This is how he and his predecessors have changed this old phrase. To help finance his so-called $4.8 billion recovery program, he will increase the 1983-1984 deficit to $31.3 billion.
Many economists tell us that there are not enough private savings or private sector moneys available to finance this deficit without interest and mortgage rates rising as they did one and a half years ago. So the Canadian consumer has another bright prospect to look forward to. In addition to record high taxes and record high unemployment, we now have record high deficits, an unsavoury epitaph in memory of a Government's term of office and one that is regarded by most Canadians today and will be regarded by many Canadians in the future as a terrible episode in Canada's history. It is a terrible nightmare that it will take us a very long time to overcome. It will take a long time to make right the terrible damage and terrible afflictions that this Government has forced upon the country and upon the people.
May 2, 1983
