subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to be able to comment on the budget statement.

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Masters
I would like to begin by talking about the amount of money that is being invested by the Government of Canada on behalf of the people of Canada to help us continue on the road to recovery. I think all Hon. Members and the country recognize that at last we seem to be on the road to recovery. Everything indicates that it will continue if we behave responsibly and recognize it will be a slow and fragile recovery.
The Government has put out $4.8 billion in investment money to try to assist that recovery as appropriately as possible. The danger in tossing big figures around is that they sound impressive and certainly a great of capital is going back into the system.
What pleases me about the budget is that the Minister has recognized that all we can do is take funds and try to use them for leverage in the private sector so that we can have a permanent recovery with permanent jobs that will last for many years to come. We recognize, even though we do not always articulate it, that Government by itself can do very little to create long-term jobs and that they must come from the private sector. As a nation we must have confidence in our ability to look after ourselves and compete in world markets.
While a great deal of money goes into immediate job creation-and I will go into the reasons why I think that is appropriate in a moment-I think that is one of the salient features of the budget. It is part of a necessary trend in the country that 1 hope will continue. It is part of the consultation process.
The truth, whether we are being politically partisan or worrying about our vested interest as businessmen, as labour leaders or educators, is that there is a tendency to fall into the trap of working in a vacuum. We know that it cannot work that way but we all have our individual horse to ride. We have to be concerned with whatever our constituency might be.
In the long run it takes a lot of honest disagreement to come together in the right forum of discussion, starting with the idea that we agree to disagree but will still communicate with each other so that a consensus can be reached. We can then start to move in the direction of looking after the common good of most of the people in Canada.
1 believe we see, to a very large degree, the fruits of the proper consultation that has taken place across Canada in the last budget. Many Hon. Members feel that they are part of the consultation process, as I do having had the opportunity to work with many groups in my constituency of Thunder Bay-Nipigon and to hear their concerns and ideas and transmit those to the Government. 1 believe that some of those ideas and thoughts are represented in a budget that makes a lot of good sense to the people of Canada. It is not perfect, but there is not much perfection in this world as yet, Mr. Speaker.
I think people have recognized that a budget has been put together that takes steps to try to create jobs immediately and do the necessary work to put the country in a position to do better in the future and to create long-term jobs. It has also established a climate whereby business, labour, Government
and educators can work together to create those jobs and build upon the upturn that we see in the economy.
There are many general benefits to Canada in this, Mr. Speaker. The consultation process is one very important and often overlooked device that has been improved upon in the budget. We are concentrating on putting Canada in a position of better competition. We are going to build the infrastructure of the country in such a way that we can better serve the people we want to serve. More important, as a trading nation we are doing those things that will put us in a more competitive position to meet the changes that are rapidly taking place in international trade.
As a trading nation I think the fact that the budget addresses ways to help us identify new markets is very basic. It will help us to be more competitive in finding those markets and it will help us be more sophisticated in our approaches to foreign trade in more parts of the country. Thunder Bay is a world port, a national port, the second busiest in Canada, so it is very much concerned with what happens in world trade.
During the economic downturn many people have asked why we blame our problems on people offshore. When you live in a part of the world where about 80 per cent of the product goes offshore, whether it be to the United States or to other nations of the world, you begin to realize that you are a part of a global community. You welcome items in the budget that will help the Export Development Corporation to be more aggressive, to work more closely with the manufacturers and suppliers of services in regions such as Thunder Bay. You also become very interested in DRIE which is the device that will bring together the indicators in the economic field that will more properly address the regions of the country and help them share in the development of industry. It will play a major part in the economy of Canada but will also be available to the people of the regions who are alert enough to want to secure export markets.
To digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, let me say that throughout this budget and other budgets there is a threat that has to be remembered and that is, that Government can do certain things to help but the prime motivator of the economy is the entrepreneurial spirit that is present in the business community with labour leaders and educators, and that is important. Therefore 1 would urge people in my region and in other regions of the country to seek ways to work in harmony by utilizing existing Government programs, examining options in business that will lead to future development, remembering all the while that it takes the entrepreneurial spirit of the people of Canada to achieve this. That, in turn, will bring about the long-term receovery that we want and will help us face an even more confident future.
The national training program and the additional moneys going to help youth is a very important aspect of the budget. We will make that money available to students who have to borrow in order to complete their education. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has identified the need to work harder with the young people of the country so that we will find options and be able to look confidently to
May 2, 1983

the future. I think we cannot spend enough money in that area. There is never enough money for it. As a nation, we must look at how we treat our youth, how we encourage them and what values we give them so that they can join in the spirit of the entrepreneur and be able to find their future.
I should like to speak about some of the comments I have received in Thunder Bay and northwestern Ontario about the budget. In all honesty, I have to tell you that the comments by and large have been very positive from all groups. We will always have an element that wishes for more, but there are some measures in the budget on which I should like to comment. There are efforts to stimulate home building, home renovation; for example, the allowance within the budget that first-time purchasers, if they are not ready to buy their home right now, will be able to buy furniture and appliances. These stimulation methods have been applauded, Mr. Speaker, not because of what they do right now but because of what they will accomplish in the future. Home construction and apartment construction have increased in Thunder Bay and are continuing to do so. That is the kind of enterprise which really turns on the economy in a fast way and in the short term. I can see our sawmills becoming busier, our retailers becoming more active. I can see the very positive effects of a sudden upturn in the sale of homes, whether brand new homes or resale homes. Once people start moving in that direction, the spin-off effect is well known. That is happening now in northwestern Ontario, and that is why I am happy to see that the budget zeroed in on that crying need for housing.
A while back a comment was made about the shipbuilding program. We have a shipyard in Thunder Bay and 1 have been in contact with them to ensure that they will be alert in bidding for any new contracts which will be forthcoming. However, I would just like to make a point about programs such as the shipbuilding program which is getting under way in Canada. It is not always possible to target the money to a specific yard. The important thing to remember, however, is that once that industry becomes busy, such as the Collingwood yard, then Thunder Bay automatically becomes busier. I would hope that some of the direct orders can be placed in our particular yard, although that would depend upon a number of factors; the position of the yard to compete for a particular program, its desire to get into it, and so on. But as soon as one very important sector of the economy, such as the shipbuilding industry, becomes busy, all yards gain. So that program, besides answering a very particular need right now, will do many parts of Canada great good because whether a shipyard receives a direct order or not, it will still benefit from that program.
Recently, Mr. Speaker, a seminar on forestry was held in Thunder Bay called "Focus on Forestry". All these people were gathered in Thunder Bay, educators, environmental people, labour people, as well as six Ministers. We invited everyone we could think of who would be interested in the forestry industry, an industry which forms so much of the wealth of northwestern Ontario and of Canada. We had a
The Budget-Mr. Masters
long, serious discussion to see how the Government of Canada could become more involved in encouraging that particular industry, and we have seen some positive results. One of the items discussed was the need to provide more protection for our forests, to protect them from disease, to protect them from fire, and so on. Therefore, the purchase of more water bombers, which was announced, is very important to the forest industry in northwestern Ontario, as well as to all of Canada. We see annually too many of our trees going up in smoke which could be used to better serve the economy of this nation. 1 would like to see many more things come out of the "Focus on Forestry" seminar and I detect signs of that in the budget.
The community of Nipigon is most interested in a forestry research station for northwestern Ontario. Quite naturally, they would like to see it in Nipigon, and so would I, if it is at all possible. 1 believe that we have to spend more money on forestry research. Whether or not it is located specifically in Nipigon-although I make the plea for it to go to that community-the main point is that the Government of Canada is moving more and more into increasing its already fairly substantial assistance to the forest industry. Research will be of great benefit to the entire forestry industry in Canada. Forgive me if I sound parochial, but I would be pleased to see northwestern Ontario considered as the site for such an enterprise.
Northwestern Ontario has several universities. Lakehead University is already benefiting from increased dollars going into forestry research through programs which it has in place. I would like to see more done in that area, and I make the pitch for Thunder Bay and northwestern Ontario simply because we have such a large percentage of that industry. 1 believe, however, that there are other economic benefits for the forest industry which are inherent in the budget, and that is that we are encouraging people to examine ways to manufacture more products for various industries, including the pulp and paper industry. What I believe is happening as a result of the budget is an upturn in the economy. People are finding more confidence in themselves and saying, "We have gone through difficult times. It is now time to go ahead." Since the budget, I have received a large number of representations from business people within northwestern Ontario, and I am pleased to say there is a very positive response from various levels of Government, asking, "How can we work with you? How can we help you to develop this new product line for the pulp and paper industry? How can we help you to export your lumber products, your paper products more efficiently to points around the world?" I also have found that the business community, in line with the budget, is saying, "We have to expand our thinking. We have to think of finding a better balance of markets around the world." That is an area where we can more properly work with the federal Government, and that industry is beginning to do so. I believe that that is materializing out of the budget. However, the budget itself, Mr. Speaker, is a guide.
I believe we in northwestern Ontario have already recognized that there is much good in the budget, and that there is

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mrs. Cossitt
room for more suggestions, for more improvements. I am hearing from constituents on that score also. 1 believe we must recognize that the budget has tried to identify where the most good could be done for the business community of Canada, to help create permanent jobs while at the same time not abandoning our need to maintain the social services of the nation. In that respect, the verdict seems to be "Northwestern Ontario", and it is very positive.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Questions, answers, comments?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to have the opportunity to speak today on the budget. There have been many before me who have spoken well on measures contained in this budget, putting forth excellent argument in favour of it and also about what the budget fails to do. I do not profess to be an economist. Indeed, many in this Chamber are not. The Chamber is made up of Hon. Members with various areas of expertise. However, as the elected Member for Leeds-Grenville, 1 do feel the need to put on the record the feelings of my constituents, which indeed are the same as those of many Canadians across this country, with respect to how the measures in this budget are going to affect their lives.
Canadians have been putting up with months of frustration, dejection and hardship in the fervent hope that the much anticipated April budget would provide them with some relief. In many cases they were disappointed. Canadians were even more disappointed with the circumstances surrounding the bringing down of the budget, a budget we hoped would give Canada new direction.
After years of high unemployment, high interest rates, record bankruptcies, sky-rocketing deficits, two disastrous budgets and financial statements, it was understandable that so many voters were demanding a new, sound fiscal policy to put Canada on the road toward economic recovery. Canadians were desperately wanting to place their trust again in the Government. They were waiting to hear that, with perseverance, things would get better. The last thing Canadians wanted to hear was the call for the resignation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) because of the careless budget leak. Canadians were looking to the Minister of Finance for responsible action on their behalf, not the irresponsible action of a Minister seeking headlines. Yes, indeed, he did receive those headlines, but not the kind that he expected.
The Minister of Finance attempted to do what he could to salvage a sagging economy, a direct result of past Government policy. Of course, there are some positive aspects to the budget. Hopefully, by utilizing the private sector, we can maintain that slight progress which has been made toward economic recovery.
In introducing his budget, the Minister acknowledged the seriousness of the unemployment situation by saying, "We must do all we can to relieve the anguish and hardship that
unemployment is inflicting on Canadian workers and their families". Although the Minister would have us believe that he is genuinely concerned about the plight of so many of Canada's citizens who are struggling to survive these devastating economic times, he has failed to do more than just acknowledge this. What he has done has been to sugarcoat a budget which miserably fails in addressing this vital problem. He has done nothing to relieve the anguish and hardship being felt by unemployed Canadians.
Today unemployment is at an incredibly high rate of 12.6 per cent, according to the Government's official rate. Sadly, however, the Government has neglected and ignored the other .5 per cent of Canadians who have become so dejected and despairing that they have given up on their search for work. They are desperate people who have a right to have jobs. They are two million Canadians living in absolute fear of their futures, with no security. That does not speak well of the Government's record.
The Minister of Finance fell short when he addressed the unemployment situation and beamingly predicted that he expected the unemployment rate to continue to be over 10 per cent by the end of the fiscal year 1986-87. In other words, he was telling us that he expected we would still have high unemployment. The prediction was based on a growth rate of 4.5 per cent. If we consider the other side of the coin and do not maintain that 4.5 per cent growth rate, we will be in an even graver position.
Unemployment and its effects permeate every aspect of Canadian life. It is not only imperative to put people back to work, but also to keep them working. How can the Minister of Finance expect us to put our faith and trust in a budget which contains measures we know have failed in the past?
The job creation programs are not new. They are perhaps reorganized, but they are definitely not new. We have heard of Summer Canada Programs, Work Experience and NEED, all short-term job creation programs, and we should be considering long-term employment opportunities. These job creation programs are designed to help create jobs immediately, but experience has taught us to know better.
The NEED Program is a prime example of how quickly the Government can move on its urgent job creation initiatives. Announced last November, in 18 months it was to have started
60,000	jobs, but six months have gone by and only 10 per cent of those jobs have actually been created. It was only with the constant pressure of the Opposition that the Government was forced to come good with its promise and get these jobs started. But how many new jobs are actually being created by this program? In fact, some of these jobs are ones which, under normal circumstances, would be filled by people already employed by the federal Government or other agencies.
In a desperate attempt to make itself look good, the Government has approved projects en masse and juggled figures with abandon. One wonders again how the Government can expect the Canadian people to trust and have faith in it.
May 2, 1983

I am deeply concerned about the type of jobs the Government is creating for our unemployed. These jobs are averaging up to 20 weeks in length, just long enough to qualify the recipient for Unemployment Insurance benefits. Short-term employment might work well for students, but for a parent with mouths to feed and a mortgage to pay it will only offer temporary relief. I desperately want to see these people off the unemployment lines, as much as they do themselves, and that thought is shared by everyone in this Chamber.
Record rates of unemployment are placing a serious drain on the Unemployment Insurance fund. The Government has already added to the large deficit by borrowing money to meet the high demands of this fund. If unemployment does not drastically decrease, the Government will be required to borrow more and more to meet the ever-increasing demands. We cannot afford to continue to fuel a deficit which has already reached proportions never before known. Reducing unemployment would reduce the deficit and halt this trend which can only lead to permanent debt and ruin for Canada.
The Minister has predicted a deficit reduced from $31.6 billion this year to over $25 billion for the fiscal year 1986-87. It is certainly not a very optimistic outlook. Canada can no longer sustain an accumulated deficit which is expected to reach over $282 billion by March 31, 1987. Again, this is all based on the expected growth rate of 4.5 per cent being achieved.
Of special concern to me are the youth of our country. Over 30 per cent of our young people will be unemployed this year, a disastrous situation for the future of our great nation. Without the energy and new ideas of our young people, Canada has no future. As that energy stagnates, enthusiasm wanes and new ideas crumble into a feeling of frustration and anger, with Canada's future becoming bleaker and bleaker.
The future of Canada is in the youth of today, and they need all the encouragement that we can provide. However, the economics of youth unemployment are matched only by the devastating social and psychological effects of this constant struggle on hundreds of thousands of young people who are just plain giving up. Soon we will be faced with a massive group of young people with no spirit, drive, ambition or experience. We cannot continue to allow them to pay for the effects of a sluggish economy. We should be nurturing the minds and spirit of our young because they hold in their hands Canada's future. They need optimism to meet their dreams and ideals, and opportunities to allow them to utilize their initiative. We must be very careful not to stifle their natural willingness to produce. They, too, were hoping once again to be able to replace their dejection over the Government with faith and hope contained in measures in the budget. The Government has recognized the problem and budgeted $95 million for wage subsidies for employers who take on young workers on an internship basis to provide training.
Even the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has said that the youth employment situation was to reach a danger point this fall when new graduates would
The Budget-Mrs. Cossitt
discover their job prospects were very scarce. Let us hope that this program will help to head off that very grave situation.
Let us consider what the Minister included in his budget which would supposedly bring about immediate employment. The new Special Recovery Capital Projects which are being announced faster than the notices can be printed are supposedly to be of high priority and of an urgent nature. However, the first of these projects will not get under way until next fall, six months from now. This is the Minister's response to the serious situation facing two million Canadians. Most of them cannot afford to sit around and wait until next fall for jobs.
In his speech, the Finance Minister indicated his support for incentives to the private sector to help it increase productivity and create long-term jobs. It is only by restoring consumer and investor confidence that Canada can once again begin to grow. Fortunately, the Finance Minister has taken heed of the many economists and the Opposition Members who have stated time and time again that the key to economic recovery is in the private sector. We now have a Finance Minister who is willing to put his faith and trust in the private sector.
However, his incentives for small business do fall short of achieving the stimulus needed to promote growth. He has, in effect, ignored the desperate financial state of many of our small businesses today. Businesses which are already on the verge of bankruptcy cannot go out and spend money they do not have on new equipment to get a tax credit. We have what I call a "spend now pay later budget". On the one hand there are incentives to stimulate the housing industry and provide employment. Fortunately we are already beginning to see the effects of that incentive since real estate is beginning to pick up appreciably. On the other hand, the Finance Minister will curb that stimulus by imposing a one per cent increase on the cost of construction materials.
We are also receiving a left handed stimulus through the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan where funds can be withdrawn from the plan to purchase items for the home without being subject to income tax, thereby stimulating the need for products and services, but next year we will see that stimulus curbed with the imposition of a one per cent increase in the federal sales tax.
We all know that revenues are desperately needed to meet the spending needs of the Government but I question the way with which this Government is collecting those revenues.
The best way to increase Government revenues is by putting people back to work, having them contribute to the public trough and stimulating the need for services and products through their increased purchasing power. Of course, the means of doing this is the most difficult task of all, but I believe there are many areas that have not been looked into with a view to realizing this goal. As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges), so adequately pointed out earlier, the tourism industry was sadly neglected and the farming community received an additional $100 million

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mrs. Cossitt
through the Farm Credit Corporation to finance farmers who are already in debt.
The Finance Minister's task is not easy and his budget can only succeed if the people of this country have trust and faith in their Government. A budget which was brought down in the manner that it was has destroyed that faith and trust and destroyed the confidence which Canadians were hoping to regain. A budget that had the possibility of doing so much for the confidence of Canadians lost it when it was brought down with the shuffling of figures to bail out a Finance Minister's reputation.
In conclusion, I want to read into the record a copy of a letter that had been addressed to the Minister of Finance. It was sent to me and I feel that it expresses very well the opinion of many Canadians. It says:
It is 8:22 p.m. April 19/83 and it is in utter frustration and desperation that I write this letter to express my total humiliation at your disgusting performance of the past 24 hours. Very briefly put, you have leaked a budget on Monday evening and in Parliament, in front of the entire Canadian populace, told me that you 'were forced' to change certain figures to take care of your 'fiscal responsibility'. Just to fully insult me, you laughed at me while you heard the honourable (compared to you and your band of hoodlums) Opposition express their disgust at your actions.
All this while, after doing nothing for any business community in this country except tax them more and more for Monique Begin's social handouts, you hand me a $31 billion deficit budget, higher than world price oil costs, endless expansion of the bilingual Civil Service and day to day demonstration of the Liberal inability to operate in any but a cover-up mode.
You and your Government are beyond words. You are living proof that absolute power corrupts absolutely.
In total seriousness-
He signed his letter. His wife added a P.S. which is very indicative of the feelings across Canada. It reads:
If my husband and I ran our household like you run our country, we would be out on the street in rags. The Liberal Party's complete arrogance in their attitude towards the people who support them through taxes, leaves me aghast. My only weapon is my vote and you can be sure I will use it.
I conclude with those comments which I do feel have been very indicative of the lack of trust, confidence and faith that the Canadian people have in their present Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the hon. lady's speech with a great deal of interest. I found that her comments were very objective and thoughtful for the most part and, taking into account the necessary partisan attitude that must be taken in this place, tended to be very constructive.
However, the letter which she read from one of her constituents tended, in my view, not only to be rather inappropriate but undoubtedly motivated by philosophies that the hon. lady just does not share. By reading that letter is she attempting to indicate that she supports the comments and allegations that are made within that particular letter?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Minister's comments with respect to my remarks. This letter was sent to me but it was addressed to the Hon. Minister of Finance. Of course it would be interesting to learn of the response that he has given to my constituent.
While I may be very objective in my view of the measures contained in the budget, I do agree with many of the views contained in this letter, such as that the budget does miss some very important ways to bring about continued employment in Canada.
The letter is here, if the Hon. Minister has challenged its content and validity. If he would confer with the Hon. Minister of Finance, I am sure that he could get a copy of that letter from his files.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question was whether the hon. lady agreed with the comments made in that letter. There are two areas in it which, in my view, she would want to reflect upon. One concerns the author's remarks which indicated that he considered the social security system in Canada as being "Begin's handouts", if memory serves me correctly. The second area was with reference to the Government's misspending funds for bilingualism. Knowing the area from which the hon. lady comes, I trust that that may be a popular view. 1 was wondering if those were her views?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the general thrust of this letter is certainly one with which I agree. The Hon. Minister brings up the matter of bilingualism. As he well knows, in the area of Leeds-Grenville that I represent, bilingualism has been a very volatile issue. It is an issue that I would not want to comment on at this particular time because it cannot be dealt with adequately in a space of a minute or two. It encompasses a great deal, not just with respect to bilingualism in the Public Service but to the whole aspect of unity within Canada, both of French and English Canadians. As I said, it cannot be commented on adequately in a couple of minutes' time.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Claude Malepart (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be taking part in the debate on the Budget that was brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on April 19 of this year.
First of all, I would like to congratulate the Minister of Finance, for two reasons. My first reason is that before bringing down his Budget, the Minister arranged for consultations with various socio-economic partners across the country, during which he met with directors of financial institutions, heads of large corporations and small- and medium-sized businesses, and labour officials across Canada. Secondly, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance for having brought down a Budget that not only meets the needs and aspirations of all Canadians but also, and first and foremost, deals with our main problem here in Canada unemployment since the Minister has given us a Budget aimed at economic recovery and job creation.
Mr. Speaker, the Budget contains a special recovery program that provides $4.8 billion, over the next four years, to accelerate economic recovery and provide new capital facilities that will increase competitiveness and generate the new jobs
May 2, 1983

Canadians need. The program provides $2.4 billion in investment support to stimulate job creation through the private sector. First of all, it will allow businesses fuller use of the investment tax credit, which will cost more than $1 billion.
Second, the scope of investments qualifying for the 7-percent investment tax credit is being broadened to cover heavy construction equipment, thus providing about $125 million of tax support.
Third, a special investment tax credit will be refundable and will allow companies which otherwise would have been unable to claim the present tax credit to be refunded a portion thereof, which represents a cost of about $400 million.
Fourth, a special recovery share-purchase tax credit will reduce the cost of new equity issued before 1987 by firms undertaking investments after the budget and this will cost about $240 million.
Fifth, a $300 million special recovery investment fund will be used to provide additional assistance for economic development projects of national and regional importance.
Sixth, a special recovery export financing fund will provide $180 million to help Canadian exporters.
Mr. Speaker, this program also includes public investment projects worth $2.4 billion. About 100 public projects will be implemented throughout Canada, and last Friday, I joined my colleague, the Member for Verdun (Mr. Savard) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), in announcing a $40 million investment project for the Societe du vieux port de Montreal, which will be used to build capital facilities and cycle paths and a pedestrian walk along this area. I feel that this investment will enhance tourism and create jobs, and I am sure that further announcements of this kind will be made in the Montreal area to help the people of Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, as far as employment is concerned, with a more vigorous, more dynamic and more productive private sector, new employment opportunities will be created for Canadians. The Canadian Government is trying to create an economic climate that will promote and stimulate the creation of permanent and productive jobs. However, the Government is aware that it is also necessary to provide assistance to the million and a half Canadians who are unemployed but willing to work. In 1983-84, more than $1.5 million will be spent by the Government on direct job creation. This is the largest program of its kind ever introduced in Canada, and under this program, nearly $900 million more will be spent than last year. The Canadian Government has given serious consideration to the basic needs of Canadians who have been exposed to prolonged periods of unemployment. Last October, the NEED program was an initiative that was very successful, contrary to what our Progressive Conservative colleagues may have said, and the provincial governments have also provided financial support for this job creation effort. In Quebec, however, the PQ Government has refused to co-operate. Nevertheless, Quebecers will not lose out, because the Canadian Government and all the Liberal caucusses from Quebec will see to it that
The Budget-Mr. Malepart
these funds are distributed through the job creation programs of community organizations or through the private sector.
The Government of Canada has decided to provide $280 million more for the NEED program and an additional $150 million goes to the Special Employment Initiatives Program for increased spending on employment intensive projects under existing construction programs and so on. An increase of $100 million is approved for expenditures on job creation projects under the Unemployment Insurance Act, which allows laid-off workers to continue to receive UI benefits when doing voluntary work on community projects.
The Canadian Government is meeting the needs of Canadians, despite our present economic problems. The Liberal Government has kept its promise to help Canadians who need help most. Canadian young people are among the groups that will benefit most from the Lalonde Budget. The Canadian Government has recognized the need for a co-operative strategy for manpower training involving all governments, business and workers. The purpose of this new strategy is to help ease the difficult transition from school to work. That is why the Canadian Government has decided to commit an additional $280 million to meet the needs of young Canadians who have not been able to find jobs. A sum of $60 million will be added to the Canada Student Loans Program, raising total funding to $141 million. This year, some 185,000 students will benefit from the program.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance did not forget Canadian families. The Liberal Government realizes that child care expenses can put a considerable burden on single-parent families. The child tax credit has therefore been increased in order to help families that need it most. At the present time, single parents and working mothers may deduct child-care expenses for which they have receipts, totalling $1,000 per child up to the age of 14. The Budget proposes to double that amount by raising the ceiling from $1,000 to $2,000 per child, to a maximum of $8,000 for a family. In addition, the new Budget has maintained the child tax credit. This year, it will be $343. The threshold of family income, below which the maximum credit will be paid, will be $26,330. Mr. Speaker, farmers and fishermen also stand to benefit from this budget. Although it may seem rather surprising that a Member from downtown Montreal should be referring to the benefits for farmers and fishermen, like all consumers I am well aware that by helping farmers we are helping consumers, because if the Government does not meet the needs of these people, we consumers in the urban areas would have to pay more for what our farmers and fishermen bring on the market.
In fact, farmers will derive benefits from the Minister of Finance's budget because an additional $100 million will be provided this year for special FCC loans to farmers in financial distress. Eligible recipients will be entitled to interest rebates of four percentage points for the first two years. A particular advantage to them will be the special provision allowing farming losses to be carried forward ten years rather

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Malepart
than the seven years applying before. Farmers and fishermen will be benefitting from the same measures, and they will now have more time to make their operations commercially viable, before the period during which losses suffered during the last year of operation can be deducted expires.
Mr. Speaker, we must not forget small businesses. Hon. Members are aware that the small business sector is one of the most important industries in Quebec as far as economic activity is concerned, and some of the proposals made by the Minister of Finance are aimed at this sector. Small businesses have always been one of the most dynamic and creative elements in the Canadian private sector. The Canadian Government wanted to do something for them and allow them to take immediate advantage of all the proposals contained in this budget. With this in mind, a Special Recovery Refundable Investment Tax Credit of 40 per cent has been provided. The Government has also decided that they alone would be immediately eligible for the three-year carryback provision. Finally, there will be major changes in the terms of reference of the Federal Business Development Bank to enable it to play a more dynamic and supportive role in advising small businesses on their total financial needs and assisting them in meeting those needs. It is readily apparent that this budget is the result of intensive consultations between the Government and representatives from the private sector, labour, business and industry. Another very important area which affects every Canadian man and woman is housing. In his budget, the Minister of Finance has committed $335 million over the next 18 months to promote housing, create jobs and provide assistance to those of our fellow-citizens who are harder hit.
I am pleased that the Government has decided to allocate $30 million more to the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Plan. This increase will enable small contractors who were unable to make new housing starts during the winter to get the assistance they need and allow thousands of Canadians to buy a home. These new allocations will bring up to nearly $750 million the amounts invested by the Government in this program, which has already helped over 200,000 Canadian families to buy a home.
The Minister has also announced significant changes to the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan. These changes will encourage those who have invested in a RHOSP to use their savings to buy new homes, furnishings and appliances. The impetus already given to the housing sector will thus be maintained. Canadians will be encouraged to withdraw their savings from the bank and use that money to create jobs, promote housing starts and create a demand on the furniture and appliance market.
Last March, the annual rate of housing starts was 177,000. With the extension of the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Plan and the further incentives provided by the changes to the RHOSP's, we are confident that the level of 150,000 housing starts forecast for 1983 will be exceeded.
Another very important program, Mr. Speaker, is the Canadian Home Renovation Plan, which provides grants of up to $3,000 to people wishing to renovate their homes and
improve their housing conditions, but which is also very effective in creating jobs. Indeed, $120 million of extra funding were announced by the Minister of Finance, bringing total new investments to $480 million. This will create 20,000 new jobs, and the average income of families benefiting from the program ranges from $20,000 to $24,000. Moreover, an additional amount of $40 million was added to the very important Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. The RRAP is helping low income families maintain their homes in adequate health and safety conditions. Certainly all Members here recognize the importance of that program and will welcome as I do the extra $40 million to be expended over the next two years. In addition to creating jobs, the RRAP program helps low income families improve their homes and maintain safety standards.
There is another important aspect for low and medium income people, those I call LMIP, just like small and mediumsized businesses are referred to as SMB. The Minister of Finance has agreed to add 2,500 units to the social housing program, which will bring the total target to 25,000 units all across Canada. This represents a commitment of some $125 million to be spread out over the duration of those residential projects.
Mr. Speaker, before I conclude, I would like to remind you and Hon. Members of what the Canadian Government has done in the area of housing in Quebec. We seldom can rely on the PQ Government to show what the Government of Canada is investing or doing in Quebec, so I think it is important today to remind all of our fellow-citizens of what the Canadian Government is doing in the area of housing. First, since the inception of the Canadian Home Renovation Plan, which provides for individual grants of up to $3,000 for house renovation, that program has been available to citizens who own a single-family dwelling or what we call a duplex. I can state that in recent days, further to the representations made by my caucus colleagues from the Montreal area where the so-called triplex and quadriplex buildings are popular, I have asked the Minister and the management of the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation whether the program could not be amended in order that a larger number of people may use the program. I can state that since its inception, the program has helped well over 14,000 families for a total expenditure of $24,332,000.
I should mention another very important program, intended for the renovation and improvement of housing throughout Quebec, namely the RRAP program, involving as it does 13,294 families for a total of $42 million in the Province of Quebec alone. Those two programs have been set up to improve housing conditions and create jobs.
I also wish to point out another really efficient program accepted by Canadians, by Quebecers generally, that is the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Plan. Indeed, since its inception, 45,000 families have taken advantage of the program thanks to $135 million in grants earmarked for Quebec.
May 2, 1983

An Hon. Member, that is my colleague from Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne) has pointed out that the Loginove Program in Quebec seems to be effective. I wish to say to my colleague that under the Canada Home Ownership Stimulation Plan, 30,025 new housing units have been financed. Recently I read a report where with reference to a statement made by a spokesman of C.N.T.U. Construction, it was pointed out that the Loginove Program had been a fiasco since the construction of 50,000 units had been expected under that program and unfortunately there had been only 3,800 units. If we compare those 3,800 units with the 3,000 financed by the federal Government I think that the latter can be proud of having stimulated the recovery of the building industry in Quebec.
Another major program is the program for subsidized housing which is being implemented under Section 56(1) and which can be either public, that is, administrated by non profit organizations, or private, that is, administered by co-operative organizations. Part of subsidized housing becomes a provincial responsibility.
In 1982, some 6,807 housing units were built in the province of Quebec, some 3,456 of which were turned over to the Government to be used for low cost lodging or shelter. Again, unfortunately, we could not rely on our PQ colleagues, for either through dishonesty or ignorance, they never acknowledge the fact that these funds are coming from the Canadian Government. Also, there is the home building program which provided the province of Quebec with 1,000 new units at a cost of $7 million.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, and considering that my time is almost expired, I should like to say that over $245 million were spent by the Canadian Government on construction I suggest, in view of the additional funds which the Minister of Finance has provided in 1983, that there is evidence of recovery in the housing industry and better housing prospects in Canada, as a result of the Canadian Government's policies.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Hon. Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) has the floor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I wonder if the Hon. Member could advise the House of the situation in the building industry in Montreal and whether he is aware of the recent increase in the number of new starts in his own region as a result of this Government's policies in the area of residential housing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying a moment ago, statistics show that the $3,000 grant to people buying a house has certainly resulted in a significant rise in the number of housing starts in the province of Quebec. There is also collaboration between the Canadian Government and the municipalities. As an example, the City of Montreal has also established a program of grants within the framework of a project calling for the construction of 20,000 dwellings and called-and as the minister responsible for Housing said earlier, there have been meetings with representatives of the City of Montreal in order to establish some coordination in the planning for house building and renovation. Just last Friday, I had the pleasure of
The Budget-Mr. Malepart
meeting with the heads of the construction section of the FTQ and with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) in order to consider another possibility in the area of house building in Quebec-although there was a salary increase-a possibility which would help some elements of the population, some people who are experiencing difficulties in the renovation sector. I am convinced that the meeting was quite productive and will have positive results.
I gave some figures a few moments ago. If we draw a comparison with the Corvee habitation program under which 11 per cent financing over three years was then available, only 3,800 units were built under that program, whereas Quebec recorded 30,000 housing starts mainly because of the $3,000 grant per unit and thanks to the Federal Government. I think that all building associations spokesmen will agree with that. But there is another aspect which people have a tendency to forget, namely our housing rehabilitation programs which are not accounted for under housing starts. It is therefore important to recall that when we talk about housing starts we should keep in mind that a good many contractors in the home rehabilitation field create jobs which are not reflected in statistics on housing starts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my riding as well people are very interested in housing. I come from a suburban area just west of the City of Toronto. The housing industry is one of our major employers. I must say, as a quick comment, that the $3,000 grant, together with the lower interest rates last year, gave an enormous boost to the housing industry in Mississauga. It is also important to note at this stage that the continuing commitment this Government has to social housing has been very well received in Mississauga. We have an active co-operative movement, a good non-profit agency for the city and a good private non-profit organization. They take advantage of the social housing units that we have included, and the 2,500 extra were very welcome.
Can the Parliamentary Secretary tell us about some of the mechanics of the RHOSP Program for new home purchasers? Some people in my riding are very interested. On the weekend I received a complaint that it might take a month or two for this program to be set up and operated. Does the Parliamentary Secretary know when the Program will come into effect and how quickly people can start to take advantage of it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Neil
generally will be made aware of the application procedures for this program so that people will be able to benefit as early as possible from the grants the Government made available to home buyers.
Another very significant initiative is the Home Ownership Program for Canadians which is designed to spur the construction industry and under which loan insurance is available. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always find it interesting to listen to Members opposite and Government Ministers talk about what the Government has done or what their program has been. They take the credit and overlook the fact that if it was not for the taxpayer of Canada, who pays the taxes and who pays the interest on the tremendous amount of debt that this Government has incurred over the years, these programs would not be available. Therefore, the thanks should go to the taxpayers of Canada rather than to this Government.
I listened with interest on Tuesday, April 19, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) presented his budget in the House. It was interesting to hear him say that much will depend on the collective behaviour of Canadians and on the response of the private sector to the measures that he was proposing in his budget. It has taken the Government about 15 years to understand the importance of the private sector as it relates to the economy of our country.
One of the largest parts of the private sector, the free enterprise sector in Canada, is the farming community. When I came into the House to listen to the Minister present his budget, I anticipated there would be something of substance in it with respect to the farming population. Quite frankly, I was disappointed because it was not until the Minister reached page 9 of his budget that the question of farming was raised, and then it was very disappointing. Those things that Members on this side of the House and the farming community in general had hoped would be in the budget just were not there.
There were two items, basically. One is referred to on page
9.	It refers to the provision which allows farming losses to be carried forward ten years rather than the seven years applicable to other businesses. If you are not making any profit and there is no profit in sight in the immediate future, the fact that you can carry forward your losses for a period of ten years is of little satisfaction to those in financial difficulty.
The second item in the budget on page 10 refers to an additional $100 million which would be made available to the special Farm Credit Corporation loans to help farmers in financial distress. That is important. When I listened to the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) say how great the budget was with respect to the farming population, I wondered what budget he was referring to. Then I realized that he really does not represent a farming area; he represents an area in the City of Montreal, and I suspect that his knowledge of farming and of the problems that farmers and the farming community are facing today is very limited.
That the Minister of Finance has ignored agriculture in this budget is not surprising or unexpected. Over the years, agriculture has not had a high priority with the Government. This sector of our economy has been ignored by the Government despite the fact that agriculture is the backbone of our country. For example, grain sales are one of the largest factors with respect to our balance of payments.
Without a healthy agricultural economy, we cannot expect to have a healthy economy throughout the country. When agriculture is in the doldrums and things are tight in the agricultural economy, machinery manufacturers and dealers throughout the country suffer, the manufacturers of cars and trucks suffer, those in the retail trade suffer-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Increased production in the agricultural area requires research and development. What has happened in agricultural research and development over the last ten or fifteen years? The portion of the budget dedicated to agricultural research and development has increased at a rate of approximately 1 per cent per year. In other words, it has fallen behind the rate of inflation in the country over this period of time.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) does not seem to be interested in research and development. Some $9 million has been available from the Prairie Farm Emergency Fund since 1972, money that belonged to the farmers, and an attempt was made to persuade the Minister and the Govern-
May 2, 1983

ment, first, to pay interest on that money because it was in a non-interest-bearing account and, second, to turn that money over for research and development. I submitted a Private Members' Bill in the House which was referred to committee. Subsequently, the agricultural groups in the West created an association for research and development, yet it took the Minister over two years to release the funds. He said, "I do not know how we can do it. It is complicated. I would like to give you the money, but," he said, "Treasury Board says that it does not know how to do it." It was finally done two or three weeks ago. I do not know how he did it, but it was a simple process. If he had problems, all he would have to do is bring a simple Bill into the House repealing the old Prairie Farm Assistance Act and turn the money over to the research group. But he did not understand that.
Today the farmer is faced with a cost-price freeze. Grain prices are lower than they have been for many years. There have been increasing input costs year after year, not only with respect to farm machinery, fertilizer and fuel oil, but everything the farmer buys has gone up in price. Yet the price of grain has gone down. It is becoming increasingly harder for the farmer to carry on.
One of the biggest features of input costs to many farmers has been interest costs, which in many cases have been as high as 25 per cent. Even the Farm Credit Corporation, a body that was set up to enable farmers to borrow on relatively easy terms, was charging interest rates in excess of 16 per cent. Presently that rate is down, of course, to 12.125 per cent. On the other hand, farmers who borrowed money from the Farm Credit Corporation at those high interest rates are locked into them for ten, 15 and even 20 years.
Doing a quick calculation, Mr. Speaker, it means that on an acre of land at a purchase price of $1,000 an acre with an interest rate of 12.125 per cent the interest per year is $121.25. The farmer will not receive $5 a bushel for his wheat this year, but if you consider the price of wheat as being $5 a bushel, he would require a yield of 25 bushels to the acre to pay the interest alone on the purchase price of that acre of land. The farmer would have to farm his land on a continuous crop basis in order to generate enough money on an annual basis. Most farmers operate on a two-year crop rotation cycle. They summerfallow half and they crop half. In other words, only half of the farmer's land is producing grain in any one year. If this is the case, then you must double the yield on that land. At a 12.125 per cent interest rate on land for $1,000 an acre, a farmer would have to produce 48 bushels per acre just to pay the interest. He would not be paying anything on the principal, he would not be covering his fuel costs, his fertilizer costs or the other input costs.
Interest rates have been a concern of our Party for many years. Over the years, we have put forth proposals to the Government and to the Farm Credit Corporation that would see the Farm Credit Corporation acquire money at very reasonable rates so it could loan it to the farmer at probably half the rate being charged at the present time. We recommended the agri-bond program whereby an individual in the
The Budget-Mr. Neil
farming area or a retired farmer could lend money to the Farm Credit Corporation at a low interest rate on the basis that the interest that he received would not be taxable, or at least would be taxable at a lower rate than normal. We also recommended a capital gains investment program whereby a retired or retiring farmer would invest the capital gains portion of the selling price of his land with the Farm Credit Corporation at a low interest rate for a period of, five years and the capital gains tax would be waived. Sucft programs would eliminate the need for the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow offshore. This is precisely what it did. On February 21, 1983 the Minister of Agriculture, through the Farm Credit Corporation, made this announcement, and I quote him as follows:
Agriculture Minister Eugene Whelan today announced that Farm Credit Corporation Canada has undertaken its first venture in the international capital markets.
FCC has issued $50 million worth of notes at 12'/s per cent due March 31, 1993. The notes are non-callable prior to maturity and have been listed on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange.
The Farm Credit Corporation has tied itself to 12'/s per cent for ten years. The Government has refused to consider the recommendation from this side of the House for the agri-bond program or the capital gains investment program. This means that the Government is prepared to subsidize offshore lenders, probably for a period of ten years, but is not prepared to consider cheap money from a source where it is readily available.
It is interesting that before the budget came down the Minister of Agriculture and the Manager of the Farm Credit Corporation appeared before the Agriculture Committee and were questioned with respect to the agri-bond and the capital gains investment programs. We asked if there was any possibility that these programs, a combination of them or some other relief, would be dealt with in the budget. While they said they were not privy to the budget, they indicated that they had made presentations to the Minister of Finance with respect to these programs and were optimistic that something would be in the budget to enable the Farm Credit Corporation to obtain funds within this country at a low rate of interest, in this way enabling it to service the farming population. It must have been a great disappointment to them when they listened to the budget speech on April 19 and learned that there was nothing in it with respect to these programs. It would appear to me that the Government is more interested in subsidizing foreign lenders than it is in doing a proper job for the farming community.
I spoke earlier about the cost-price squeeze with respect to farmers and about low grain prices. A short time ago the Minister in charge of the Wheat Board announced a reduction in the initial price over the previous year. As well, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) made an announcement which indicated that the cost of transporting grain from western Canada to the shipping points would double in three years and would increase five times by the year 1990. If the Government continues in power and continues to ignore the agricultural

May 2, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Neil
community it will do a great deal of harm to those people who are the backbone of the country.
I hope that the Minister and Members of the Government will give some thought to what can be done to help the agricultural community. I assume that this Session of Parliament will end shortly and that we will have a Speech from the Throne in the fall. I hope that by that time the Government will have listened to some of the advice and the pleas offered by Members on this side on behalf of the farmers.

subtopic: CHARTER OF RIGHTS-ADMINISTRATION COSTS. THE CONSTITUTION-COST OF PATRIATION
CHARTER OF RIGHTS-ADMINISTRATION COSTS. THE CONSTITUTION-COST OF PATRIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 17, 1982 I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) what the total cost was going to be for administering the Charter of Rights and repatriating the Constitution. The Minister of Justice would not give us the cost. I followed up with a question to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) as to whether he had conducted a cost-benefit analysis in these instances. Again, I did not receive an answer. Canadians have a right to answers regarding how their tax dollars are being spent, and for what reasons. They also have a right to know what, if any benefits Government expenditures will give them.
May 2, 1983

The Auditor General has said that the Government has lost control of the public purse. The Auditor General has also reported sloppy accounting practices in the Government. The estimated deficit for the fiscal year 1983-84 was $29 billion. But, with the new budget, the Liberal Government has once again broken its record. The projected deficit is now $31.3 billion. Negligence on the part of the Government has given rise to various inefficient and costly Government policies. Cost-effectiveness is not a consideration.
On November 9, 1976 I cautioned the House that the Government should investigate Canadair expenditures. I also said the Government should table all documents regarding Canadair aircraft and how many tax dollars are committed to Canadair.
On December 2, 1976 I warned the Government again of Canadair's disaster course. I said the Government should come clean and state its plans and expectations for Canadair and that the Government should start revealing true information about Canadair's financial position.
On February 24, 1977 I moved that the then Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce be instructed to appoint an independent committee to investigate the structural problems Canadair was then experiencing with production of new aircraft.
Here I am again, seven years later, reiterating my warning. Once again, the Government is bailing out Canadair, another Crown Corporation, which is, and has been, on a disaster course. Last fall Canadair's financial assets were turned over to another Government-owned company, the Canada Development Investment Corporation. Since that time a financial report has been prepared but the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has refused to make it public. The Prime Minister has told Canadians that "We would be on the road to financial disaster if nothing was done to bring spending under control". In spite of these comments, the Liberal Government is allowing further funding of this Crown Corporation which has consistently mismanaged its finances. We now learn that Canadair is planning to lay off 570 people by mid-July. The taxpayers' bill to bail out Canadair will amount to $2.3 billion.
The Liberal Government has lost control of spending. The taxpayer does not know where his tax dollars are going. The Liberal Government's lack of accountability and lack of cost-benefit analysis has been reported time and time again by the Auditor General. In 1962, there were only 28 Crown Corporations, controlling $8.4 billion in assets. Today there are over 300 Crown corporations controlling $67 billion in assets. Revenues of Crown corporations in the most recent fiscal year were $31.9 billion and expenses were $33.6 billion.
In 1982, the Auditor General reported the following concerning Crown corporations:
Most corporations are virtually known even to the best informed members of the tax paying public. Yet.. . they represent a hole in the taxpayer's pocket... a consistent negative return on investment.
Adjournment Debate
There are no adequate provisions for Parliament to review the budgets of over 300 corporations in which the Canadian public has an interest.
The next excerpt from the Auditor General's report of 1982 is a true representation of what is occurring in Canadair, innumerable other corporations and, no doubt, in many federal Government departments and agencies:
Without public exposure, the temptation is overwhelming to send good money after bad in the hope of reversing the situation, no matter how hopeless the situation has become-
The Progressive Conservative Government wanted tighter control over Crown corporations by Government. We started introducing legislation to act upon the recommendations along these lines from the Lambert Commission, the Auditor General and the Public Accounts Committee. As we were defeated, we could not implement the legislation.
The Government owned Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation wasted more than $20 million in public funds developing a computer system which was technically impossible to use.
On April 26, 1982, I informed the House that the National Energy Program drove investment out of the country, which resulted in a loss of approximately 60,000 jobs across Canada. The Liberal Government could not possibly have been considering cost effectiveness when implementing this program.
As the House is aware, the Liberal Government and the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal) made public their intention to make Canada a French state. Cost benefit analysis has received absolutely no consideration in this regard, as demonstrated by the Secretary of State in the following excerpt from his speech:
Francophone rights cannot be bought, sold, substracted from, divided or multiplied in terms of dollars and cents in the budgets of a troubled economy, and that will apply, I promise you, for as long as I am Secretary of State of Canada. If I have to cut back some programs-and I've already done so-there is one area in which I have no intention of using the scissors: the advancement of Francophone rights in Canada. Another thing that needs to be said: as we say in French, "like it or not", it is going to take a little more money-
There has been no White Paper or Green Paper on the proposal to make Canada a French state, and no permission from the Canadian people. In the future, all Government programs should have a cost benefit analysis done before being implemented.

My second question related to the international agreement in the absence of ratification. Canada indicated in early March that if the U.S.A. could not or would not implement the Treaty's terms on a provisional basis in 1983, nor would Canada. Therefore, on April 27, 1983, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans announced fishing plans for 1983 that are not entirely consistent with the treaty. This action was taken after careful consideration and discussion with the industry advisers who had served as members of the Canadian negotiating team. Many of these advisers have been part of the delegation since negotiations began in 1970.
Canada's action in not implementing the treaty could have significant effects on the conservation of chinook salmon in particular.

Unless a treaty can be put in place, Canadian catches of salmon bound for the U.S.A. are likely to increase, and our catches of our own Fraser River sockeye and pink salmon will far outweigh expectations in the U.S.A., which normally shares that harvest inside Juan de Fuca Strait.
Canada remains hopeful that accommodation can be reached, but the United States cannot expect Canada to accept unbalanced changes to a treaty which took much effort to negotiate and demanded many compromises.
